title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
abstract: November 24, 2026 Science Publication GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities Read the paper (opens in a new window) Share Key findings: Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing. The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools. Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does. Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical. Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements. Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs. Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested. A closer look at our models’ protein designs We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness. The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction. The model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together. With our research partner, Onava ⁠ (opens in a new window) , we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals. Laboratory Experiment 1: Designing small proteins that bind to a target Our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets. We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models. To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target. GPT‑6.2 designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to chosen targets. Specialized models then proposed amino acid sequences—the order of the proteins’ chemical building blocks—and helped select designs for our research partner Onava to make and test in the lab. We tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target. We found 5 hits for PD-L1 (a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system), 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. The original RFdiffusion study ⁠ (opens in a new window) reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. Nevertheless, our results provide early evidence that we can turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins that bind to their intended targets in the lab. An internal research model designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to the target proteins shown in gray.

title: Searching for distant planets with Astra
abstract: An illustrated view of HD 164604 b zooms out to the Milky Way. Boxes mark a selection of systems with confirmed exoplanets. Distances are scaled to the zoom and show the distance from Earth at the widest view. Hover over or tap a box to read its label. Use the arrow keys to browse labels and Escape to dismiss them. November 24, 2026 Science Searching for distant planets with Astra Two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to look for signs of planets in public telescope data. Now they’ve given professional astronomers a few places to look more closely. Share Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system ⁠ (opens in a new window) since the first ones were announced in 1992 ⁠ (opens in a new window) . A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers. *Data from the NASA Exoplanet Archive’s Planetary Systems Composite Parameters table ⁠ (opens in a new window) . 2026 data are year to date through November 24, 2026. How astronomers discover exoplanets Astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope ⁠ (opens in a new window) that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. When the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90 ⁠ (opens in a new window) . Now, tools like Astra are helping amateur astronomers design and run searches of their own, often on data that has already yielded the more obvious exoplanet signals. Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, came to astronomy through his love of photographing the night sky. He used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope, a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018. Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, has always loved astronomy. Working independently of Bond, he tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars. Both searches identified potential exoplanets. Bond and Byrd have now turned to astronomers for an independent assessment of their results. Bond contacted an astronomer at the SETI Institute, who ran an independent search and found two of the same signals in the Kepler data. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. It’s in line for further analysis, and two more candidates are awaiting submission. Looking for dips in starlight One of the most common ways to find an exoplanet is to watch the star it orbits. When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view on Earth, it blocks a tiny amount of starlight. Astronomers call that crossing a transit. On a graph of the star’s brightness over time, known as a light curve, a transit shows up as a dip. If the dip keeps coming back at regular intervals, astronomers know when to watch for it again. Searching for that pattern across thousands of stars is partly a coding problem. Astronomers have published methods for picking out faint, recurring dips in years of measurements. Bond used Codex to compare those methods, combine them in a search program, and test whether changes to the code improved the search. One AI agent scanned the light curves for promising signals. Another ran more detailed checks on the candidates the first one flagged. Bond ran the program on public data from the Kepler Space Telescope. The search flagged more than 200 signals, including 10 from previously confirmed planets. Finding those known planets gave Bond confidence that the program could pick out the kinds of signals he was looking for. Two stars stood out. The first, KIC 5689121, is a relatively cool star about half the size of our sun in the constellation Lyra. The Codex search found a dip in brightness every 13.8 days. If a planet is causing it, the amount of light it blocks suggests it could be about 2.4 times Earth’s diameter. These four curves show the same Kepler observations aligned on a 13.77-day cycle. The second star, KIC 6691030, is faint and lies in the northern sky. The Codex search found a dip in its brightness every 4.8 days, consistent with a planet smaller than Neptune. These were the two signals the SETI Institute astronomer found independently. Confirming what caused them could take months or years. “Kevin’s work shows how citizen scientists, equipped with AI, can help astronomers explore the Kepler Bonus Catalog—a vast collection of stars beyond Kepler’s original targets. His pipeline has surfaced promising candidates in data traditional searches may have missed. Our initial checks are encouraging, and follow-up observations will tell us more.” Vishal Gajjar, associate director for international SETI programs at the SETI Institute Byrd used Astra to design two searches. One looked broadly for exoplanet candidates. The other focused on stars’ habitable zones. A habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet with a suitable atmosphere could support liquid water on its surface. Byrd then asked Astra to review published methods, build the search software, and run initial checks on promising signals. His searches drew on observations from TESS, which NASA launched in 2018, and from other public telescope archives. Kepler watched one field for four years. TESS surveyed both hemispheres in its first 26 sectors, from 2018 to 2020. The star field comes from NASA’s TESS mosaic through September 2025 ⁠ (opens in a new window) , clipped to that original survey footprint. The wider gap shows where TESS pointed farther north during six observing sectors. The inset marks KIC 5689121 ⁠ (opens in a new window) in the original Kepler field ⁠ (opens in a new window) . See NASA’s final prime-mission coverage maps ⁠ (opens in a new window) and its earlier field-of-view animation ⁠ (opens in a new window) . The first pass through the data turned up 49 candidates. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on the TESS mission, where it is awaiting further analysis. His search is still running. What does it take to confirm a planet? When astronomers see a star dim, they have to consider what else might explain it. Two stars passing in front of one another can produce a similar dip. Even a change in temperature aboard a telescope can affect its instruments enough to make a star appear to dim. Astronomers can use statistics to show that an exoplanet is the most likely explanation for a series of dips. They can also collect more observations, sometimes using a different method. For example, an orbiting planet’s gravity tugs on its star, causing it to move slightly toward and away from us. That motion, called radial velocity, shows up as tiny shifts in the color of the star’s light. Astronomers then publish their findings in a peer-reviewed journal so others can examine the evidence. For Bond and Byrd, each candidate is a question that can be tested. If a planet is passing in front of the star in Lyra every 13.8 days, astronomers can watch for the next crossing. Further observations can help establish whether the dip repeats as expected, while additional checks can help determine what is causing it. Photographs by Kevin Bond Taking part in the search You can contribute without owning a telescope. NASA’s Exoplanet Watch ⁠ (opens in a new window) lets you request data and learn to plot a light curve yourself. Its broader exoplanet citizen science programs ⁠ (opens in a new window) offer other ways to participate.

title: How Intentful uses dots to make more time for growth
abstract: November 24, 2026 How Intentful uses dots to make more time for growth How a small business founder’s dot helps her with research and proposals, while alerting her to critical messages and resolving issues. Explore ChatGPT for small businesses Company size: SMB Region: North America Industry: Services Products: ChatGPT Share Marina Petrova is CEO and cofounder of Intentful ⁠ (opens in a new window) , a lean team that helps brands make their marketing interactive, with products such as ads that answer customers’ questions in real time and tools that make website information readable by AI. The company also advises and trains marketers on using AI. In travel and tourism, Intentful works with destination organizations and local businesses such as hotels, restaurants, and attractions. A custom proposal is part of how Marina wins their business, showing prospects what’s possible and what it would take to deliver. To keep Intentful growing, she needed more room for that strategic work, but she was spending too much time on research, hunting for files, and formatting decks. Her dot ⁠ changed all that, taking on tasks and meeting Marina’s needs before she even had to ask. “My dot makes me feel like I gained a new superpower.” —Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful From 300 websites to a proposal in hours instead of days For one of Intentful’s tourism clients, Marina wanted to propose a package of Intentful’s AI services for hundreds of local businesses in the destination. Before she could price the package, she needed to work out which businesses’ websites the package could cover and what Intentful had charged other clients for similar work. She brought in her dot, which she named Aria, to help her get from research to a proposal she could put her name on in a few hours instead of several days. First, Marina gave Aria a spreadsheet of URLs and criteria for deciding which sites to include. For example, a site needed a readable sitemap listing no more than 3,000 pages. “My dot looked through about 300 website sitemaps, helped me figure out which sites to include in a new offer for local businesses, and pulled pricing from past agreements.” —Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful Next, Aria helped Marina research pricing. Through ChatGPT ⁠ (opens in a new window) plugins, Aria reviewed Intentful’s sales data, including past engagements and discussions in HubSpot. It surfaced pricing from earlier agreements and context from Intentful’s plans for the following year. Using that data, Marina and Aria then built a pricing model: page counts determined the pricing tier, and previous customer agreements also informed the price. “We worked through a custom pricing model together, and then Aria turned it into a one-page proposal I reviewed and edited,” said Marina. When drafting proposals, Aria knows to use Intentful’s templates from Google Drive. Marina can also point Aria to an earlier proposal as a reference, so the draft follows Intentful’s style from the start. “I need to say what needs to be in a proposal, but I don’t need to spend an hour figuring out its layout. My dot handles that,” Marina says. Aria can also spot things Marina hadn’t thought to check. When Marina asked Aria to reuse pricing from an earlier proposal, it noticed that the original renewal date didn’t match the timing she remembered. Aria flagged the discrepancy and left the date out of the new draft. Staying ahead of messages, tasks, and team updates Marina uses the Gmail and Slack plugins in ChatGPT to catch up on conversations, find open tasks, and see where the team needs her. Aria checks for messages that need Marina’s attention. While Marina was offline, Aria spotted a reply she had been waiting for and let her know it included an invitation for a call that morning. Marina also uses Aria to talk through ideas, find conversations, check an account’s history in the CRM, or open and assign tasks in Asana. She often briefs Aria by phone while she travels. “On a long drive, I call my dot and talk through what needs to get done. We chat through updates for client proposals, and my dot already knows the structure, the formatting, and what needs to be done.” —Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful Marina loves that her dot works in the tools she already uses. When Aria writes a draft, Marina can leave comments in Google Docs exactly where she wants changes. On longer documents, she asks Aria to use suggesting mode so she can see what changed. Aria also keeps up with changes in shared work without being asked. For a conference presentation, Marina created the deck and a colleague added two slides. “Aria noticed the new slides, updated the speaker notes without being asked, and let me know,” Marina says. Marina chooses which information Aria can access and always reviews outgoing email. She can keep work moving without handing over the final call. Using dots to teach others about AI When Marina prepared an AI 101 session on agents, she used Aria to help build the lesson. The process was itself an example of what she wanted attendees to learn: delegate a real task, give the agent enough context, challenge the result, and stay in control of what goes out. Aria’s support continued even after the class. After a flight, Marina saw a participant’s request for access to a training file. When she checked with Aria, it had already shared the file. And after a session for 50 marketers, Aria noticed that a software glitch was preventing participants from opening the recording. It flagged the access issue and offered to fix it before the link was shared. “With my dot, I can focus on strategic things. I can focus on ideas and growth.” —Marina Petrova, CEO and cofounder, Intentful Join the new era of work More than 1 million businesses around the world are achieving meaningful results with OpenAI. title: How iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories
abstract: November 24, 2026 How iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories Contact sales Company size: Enterprise Region: Latin America Industry: Technology Products: API 15,000 code repositories at iFood 25,000+ runs completed by the platform US$0.04 average inference cost per run 2x+ as many vulnerabilities fixed through the security platform Share The Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. In the internal security platform, the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled. The challenge isn’t the task—it’s the scale iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories. Each periodically needs specific tasks performed: validating code to ensure it meets internal standards, fixing vulnerable dependencies, or running an analysis. None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply. “Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.” Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle. “Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.” What was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated runtime . “Teams can focus on solving their business problems and delegate execution to our platform.” —Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood A coding agent in the cloud, accessible through an API The team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that launches a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later. “The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Users can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time. The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable. Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the skills the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end. In between is the agentic execution itself, running GPT‑5.6 Luna inside the sandbox. “It’s a combination of those two things: deterministic steps and agentic execution within the workflow.” The sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes the toolchains iFood’s ecosystem requires—Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript, and Go—along with general-purpose tools. Beyond the sandbox, the agent can access Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes, and AWS. Why GPT‑5.6 Luna The model choice came down to three factors considered together, rather than just one. “We chose GPT‑5.6 Luna because, among models at the same checkpoint, the benchmarks showed it offered a great balance of intelligence, efficiency, and execution speed—how quickly it could complete tasks. Those three qualities together led us to choose GPT‑5.6 Luna.” That balance matters more for a platform built to scale than it would for a one-off use case. With tens of thousands of tokens being consumed, the average cost of four U.S. cents per run stops being a minor detail and becomes an architectural consideration. “Given our plans to scale the platform across many use cases at iFood, the balance of efficiency and intelligence that OpenAI’s model provides ensures we can scale sustainably.” —Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood How to tell whether the agent completed the task Delegating execution at scale creates a new challenge: automatically determining whether the agent did what it was supposed to do. iFood’s answer comes in the step after the session. Once execution is complete, the result is processed using OpenAI’s Structured Outputs, which requires the output to conform to a predefined contract. “We process the result using Structured Outputs, which ensures the response follows a predefined contract. From the agent’s session, we can identify the outputs within the response structure we expect. This helps reduce uncertainty and ensures we can always get a response from the agent’s session, whether positive or negative.” —Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood The first major user: security The platform already powers an internal iFood security product that scans the 15,000 repositories for vulnerable dependencies and attempts to fix them. The migration had a direct impact: “With our platform, the accuracy of those changes, those fixes, more than doubled,” says Coelho. This use case illustrates the idea behind the platform: the security team didn’t need to build its own agentic runtime or become experts in agent orchestration. It needed to call an API. Asynchronous execution gives developers their time back The team emphasizes what asynchronous execution frees developers to do, rather than replacement. Because the task is delegated and runs without supervision, the developer doesn’t have to stay focused on monitoring it. “While they’re in a meeting, they can launch a code fix, a performance analysis, or another task that’s a little more routine—something they can delegate without having to monitor it at that moment.” Routine work no longer competes for the team’s attention. That leaves time for problems that require judgment. “You can unlock those productivity gains without necessarily having to monitor the work as it happens.” —Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood Modeled on the APIs that inspired it The Remote Agents Platform was designed as an internal layer with similarities to the way OpenAI makes this type of task available to external customers. “The Remote Agents Platform drew a lot of inspiration from OpenAI’s APIs, both the Batch API and the Agents API, which is an even more recent OpenAI product. We built a platform that resembles those products, but is internal to iFood.” The inspiration went beyond the concept. It extends to the design of the interfaces, the organization of resources, and the approach to asynchronous execution with results retrieved later. “These products directly inspired how we built our solution.” —Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer, iFood Results at a glance The platform has completed more than 25,000 tasks, consuming more than 27 billion tokens, at an average cost of US$0.04 per run. After migrating to the Remote Agents Platform, the internal security platform more than doubled both the accuracy of its fixes and the number of vulnerabilities resolved. Coverage extends across iFood’s more than 15,000 code repositories. All runs use GPT‑5.6 Luna, chosen for its balance of intelligence, efficiency, and speed. Structured Outputs ensures that each session returns a result that follows a predefined contract, whether positive or negative. Product teams have moved from building fragmented solutions to delegating agentic execution through a REST API. Lessons for leaders The bottleneck is often the runtime, not the use case. Several teams already knew what they wanted to automate; they lacked an environment in which to run it. Combine deterministic steps with agentic execution. Cloning, publishing, and making artifacts available don’t require a model; the complex task in between does. Treat cost per run as an architectural decision.

title: Clay helps sales teams win with Codex and ChatGPT
abstract: November 24, 2026 Clay helps sales teams win with Codex and ChatGPT ChatGPT and Codex integrations help Clay users research deals and turn data into go-to-market plays, and GPT‑6 models handle the reasoning. Start building with OpenAI Company size: Startup Region: North America Industry: Technology Products: API, Codex, ChatGPT Share Even when sales teams have plenty of data about a prospect, they can still struggle to understand what matters most and develop a winning pitch. Clay ⁠ (opens in a new window) is a self-learning revenue engine designed to help. Using GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and other models, Clay enables users to build lists of companies and people, enrich those records using agents, and use that information in go-to-market plays. Clay also brings these capabilities to where customers are already working with plugins for Codex and ChatGPT, making it easier to create and run go-to-market workflows and research accounts and deals. “Clay in ChatGPT gives sales reps a way to understand more about the customers they’re trying to sell to. It brings all of that rich context to the places they’re already working.” —Jeff Barg, Head of AI, Clay Giving sales reps more context to act on Clay’s Codex integration lets builders create and run go-to-market plays in Codex, while giving sales reps access to data they can use to research an account or understand a deal they’re trying to close. Jeff has seen reps combine information from their own systems and public datasets to determine how to best communicate their product’s value to a customer. “Customers love using Codex for a lot of different tasks in sales,” he says. “We’ve seen the best sales reps be the most empowered by this.” Clay’s ChatGPT plugin brings the same customer data into another tool reps already use, helping them learn more about prospects without leaving ChatGPT. Jeff says, “It’s been a big success.” Matching intelligence and cost to the task OpenAI models power Claygent’s research, qualification, enrichment, and signal detection, as well as the agent that helps users build workflows and coordinate other Clay agents. Clay uses GPT‑6 Sol as its primary model, with GPT‑6 Astra for harder tasks and GPT‑6 Luna for cost-sensitive work. That range supports background research and copywriting as well as agents that users work with directly. “GPT-6 Sol is a really great model for go-to-market plays. It has really good intuition and can build long-horizon, outcome-based go-to-market tasks.” —Jeff Barg, Head of AI, Clay The Responses API lets Clay use different levels of intelligence and cost through the same interface. “Having the same Responses API across the different price points is something that’s super appealing to us with OpenAI models,” said Jeff. Building end-to-end plays that self-improve over time GPT‑6 Astra also helps Jeff build and test software. He used to spend much of his time manually checking features he had built; now he can ask GPT‑6 Astra to handle more of that work. He explains, “GPT‑6 Astra really changed how I build software because it fully closed the loop on the engineering process. Now I can have Astra write code, add tests, and then actually run the tests and test the feature and record that and upload that in the PR. It simplifies my life a lot.” For Clay’s customers, Jeff sees GPT‑Live‑1 as a way to use Clay and Codex by voice and help prospects learn about a product. Clay is working on inbound sales development features that would let an agent show a product or service to a prospect. He also sees the Decisions API as another way to integrate models into Clay and open up new use cases. Clay’s ambition is to carry go-to-market workflows from start to finish, with agents that improve as they learn from the results. For Jeff, the goal is to empower builders “to bring the same shift that happened in software engineering to go-to-market.” OpenAI <3 startups Join the community Start building (opens in a new window) Keep reading Richpanel helps companies automate 50% of support in 30 days Startup Nov 23, 2026 Hebbia sees improvements in financial research with GPT-6 Astra Nov 20, 2026 Cogent and OpenAI build cyber defense factories for enterprises Startup Nov 10, 2026

title: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton
abstract:
Back to Articles Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton Enterprise + Article Published November 24, 2026 Upvote 5 Oluwaseun Doherty seun-doherty Follow nvidia Oyindamola Omotuyi OOyindamola Follow nvidia Richard AntRi31 Follow nvidia TL;DR Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment. Introduction A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy. NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing. 1. Set Microduck obstacle avoidance in Isaac Lab For simulation and training, prepare: A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements. Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager. For physical-robot testing, prepare: A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task. A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded. A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles. Quick install Install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies: git lfs install
git clone --branch exp/microduck https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git cd IsaacLab
uv sync --frozen Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets: uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets Download the walking policy Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically. uv run isaaclab play \ --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \ --rl_library rsl_rl --checkpoint pretrained \ --num_envs 1 --visualizer none \ --video newton_gl --video_length 1 \ presets=backlash 2. Build the obstacle course The environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box , office bin , bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready. uvx --from huggingface-hub hf download nvidia/simready-assets \ --repo-type dataset \ --revision 9d4556bfe80868c1d27a7a7ba1c2774e63e8cedd \ --include "box_cardboard_a01/*" \ --include "trashCan_office_black_a03/*" \ --include "table_bedside_b01/*" \ --local-dir ./assets/simready At each episode reset, the environment code automatically samples a layout, shuffles the props, and varies their placement and rotation. Most courses scatter obstacles ahead of the duck, with a smaller mix of clear paths, barriers and passages. The code also mirrors layouts and mixes aligned and staggered rows. Goals start ahead of the duck. Movement commands guide it toward the goal while the policy adjusts them around obstacles. Figure 1. Varied obstacle-course layouts with SimReady assets and primitive geometry. 3. Understand how ToF sensing guides the walking policy The IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior. During training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment. Rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls. The obstacle-avoidance task lives in isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle . Its configuration is in obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py , ToF sensing is in sensors.py , and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under mdp/ . Model the ToF sensor MicroDuckToFCamera extends Newton’s LegacyMultiMeshRayCasterCamera to model the VL53L5CX—a compact time-of-flight (ToF) sensor on the microduck that measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz. The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck. Real recordings informed the sensor placement and floor readings in simulation. Training adds noise, delays and missing measurements—including near the grid’s edges—to expose the policy to imperfect data. The excerpt below shows selected sensor settings already included in the task configuration. You do not need to edit or run this code separately. # Selected settings; mount and raycast targets omitted. head_tof = MicroDuckToFCameraCfg( prim_path=MICRODUCK_HEAD_BODY_PATH, update_period= 1.0 / 15.0 , pattern_cfg=patterns.PinholeCameraPatternCfg( focal_length= 1.0 , width= 8 , height= 8 , horizontal_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE, vertical_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE, ), randomization=ToFRandomizationCfg( mount_pitch_degrees=(- 10.0 , 10.0 ), mount_height_m=(- 0.02 , 0.02 ), floor_validity_midpoint_offset_m=( 0.0 , 0.13 ), near_floor_edge_impairment_probability= 0.5 , ), data_types=[ "distance_to_image_plane" , "distance_to_camera" ], max_distance=TOF_MAX_RANGE, depth_clipping_behavior= "zero" ,
) 4. Train the Microduck policy across parallel environments Train the navigation policy with PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 training iterations. Its actor, critic, normalizers, and optimizer start fresh. The task configuration loads the fixed walking checkpoint, robot model, and obstacle assets. The 16,384 environments shown here are configurable, not a minimum requirement. Lower --num_envs to fit your GPU’s available memory. With fewer environments collecting experience in parallel, reaching comparable policy performance may require more training iterations and longer training time. We also trained this policy on NVIDIA DGX Spark in approximately 6 hours using 4,096 parallel environments for 3,000 PPO updates, demonstrating a smaller-scale configuration for the same workflow. Run this command to train the policy: uv run isaaclab train \ --task IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck \ --rl_library rsl_rl \ --num_envs 16384 \ --max_iterations 1500 \ --seed 42 \ --device cuda:0 \ --visualizer none \ presets=backlash Figure 2. Parallel MicroDuck obstacle-avoidance simulation 5. Inspect behavior and export the policy to ONNX Playback uses the same props, primitives, frozen walker and sensor randomization as training, with a different seed for new obstacle arrangements. Navigation checkpoints are saved under logs/rsl_rl/microduck_obstacle_avoidance_tof_flat_backlash/<timestamp>/ relative to the repository root. Choose a model_<iteration>.pt file from your run and replace /absolute/path/to/model.

title: Meet Facebook’s Your Algorithm: How Meta Turns Plain-Language Preferences Into Ranking
abstract: Meta has published an engineering deep dive on Facebook Your Algorithm . Your Algorithm lets people tell Facebook, in plain language, what they want in Feed and Reels. Meta announced the feature on October 13, 2026. The new post shows how large language models (LLMs) sit inside a production recommender. For developers, it is a rare look at explicit preferences wired into an implicit-signal ranking stack. Your Algorithm is an AI-powered preference page for Facebook Feed and Reels. It has 3 parts, per Meta’s engineering post . A one-sentence “Lately Summary” describes recent viewing. An “Interested In” list is prefilled from past activity. A “Not Interested In” list holds exclusions. Users can type interests, move them between lists, or delete them. Access is through the three-dot menu on posts, according to Meta’s newsroom . Meta’s framing is simple. Implicit engagement signals scale well but adapt slowly and miss nuance. Explicit, stated preferences close that gap. Meta splits the preference lifecycle into 4 components: Validated interests are enriched with an embedding and search keywords. They are saved to a shared store that both Feed and Reels read. A separate component runs integrity and safety checks. Each interest drives 4 retrieval sources. 2 match content directly: search and clusters of closely related topics. 2 extend reach: the content graph and item-to-item similarity. A relevance check compares the interest’s meaning with each candidate. Passing candidates get a late-stage ranking promotion. A reranking control layer then stops flooding: Meta calls this layered filtering at every stage. Ranking uses embedding comparison to remove close matches. Demotion rules push down near matches. A fine-tuned LLM reranker then reviews the final list. Quality requests, such as less AI-generated or sexually suggestive content, take a different path. They map to dedicated demotion signals, not topic matching. Requests naming a creator filter that creator directly. On the client, cache invalidation removes queued items that match a new exclusion before display. The reranker is trained to return only the items to remove. Meta says this small fine-tuned model beat a general-purpose model judging each item. It was faster and more reliable. Outputting a short removal list is cheaper than scoring every candidate. Speed comes from a “supplementary tail load.” Adding an interest fires an extra fetch outside the normal cycle. Meta gives no latency figure for it. Source conflict: YouTube’s Help Center says 1 custom feed at a time. TechCrunch reports multiple feeds rolling out from October 2026. Check out the Meta engineering post and the Facebook announcement . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . title: OpenAI and Cisco Releases Shirudo: An Open-Source Linux Runtime Allowing Agents to Defend Systems Without Downtime
abstract: OpenAI and Cisco have released Shirudo , an open-source Linux runtime for defending live systems. Shirudo is an eBPF runtime that lets AI agents write temporary “shields” against known exploits. Shields block the vulnerable behavior while legitimate requests keep flowing. Teams get time to test and ship the real patch. The engineering came from Isovalent at Cisco , the team behind Cilium and Tetragon. Patching takes time. OpenAI team notes that testing and deploying a fix can take days or weeks. Blocking a whole Linux operation is risky, because exploits and normal requests often share it. Shirudo targets that patch window. Shirudo uses eBPF, which runs small verified programs at hooks inside the Linux kernel. The name is Japanese for “shield.” Isovalent calls it a rewrite of Tetragon , its 2022 eBPF security platform. The design splits work across 2 roles: A shield can do 3 things. It can block the code path a bug needs, replace vulnerable code, or add detection visibility. The docs call these packages upatches : small BPF C programs shipped as signed artifacts. There is deliberately no policy DSL. The Linux Plumbers talk by Daniel Borkmann and John Fastabend says agents work better with code directly. Isovalent describes 4 stages, with Codex as the control plane: Operators approve shields before enforcement. Teams can also observe a shield’s impact before it blocks anything. The kernel checks each loader’s signature against a .bpf keyring. The eBPF verifier then checks program safety. A TPM 2.0 records every load and unload, and signs attestation evidence. The test bundle uses an ML-DSA-87 signing key, a post-quantum algorithm. Registry traffic uses TLS 1.3 with hybrid post-quantum key exchange. Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap corruption bug in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. It scores 9.2 on CVSS 4.0. It affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI. Calif.io found it on October 24 using Codex. Oracle shipped a fix on November 17. Codex generated a guard on java.util.Base64$Decoder.decode0 . It was attached to a running Elasticsearch 9.5.5 node. The exploit input was rejected and the service stayed up. That is the only disclosed test. No false-positive rate or overhead figure was published. Source note: OpenAI frames shields as eBPF. The Isovalent post says this specific shield was Java bytecode. The Java agent docs call such upatches an in-application mitigation, not a kernel boundary. Those docs also describe startup-time loading only, while the demo attached at runtime. Requirements are strict. Per the system requirements page : There is no fallback for older kernels. Developers can try the VM quickstart or the Isovalent lab . Check out the OpenAI announcement , Isovalent technical post , GitHub repo and docs . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension .
