title: How to Run Inkling 2 Mini Locally on an RTX 3090 Using Unsloth Studio
abstract: How to Run Inkling 2 Mini Locally on an RTX 3090 Using Unsloth Studio American open-source AI is making a comeback, and this powerful local LLM is proving that fast inference, AI coding agents, and impressive results don't require expensive APIs. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on November 24, 2026 in Language Models We finally have a serious American competitor to Qwen3.8-27B, one of the best AI models you can run locally. Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Mini , a powerful open-weight model that matches Qwen3.8-27B on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and even outperforms it on several coding, agentic, and tool-use benchmarks. What makes this release particularly exciting is its efficiency. Inkling 2 Mini has 26 billion parameters, but its Mixture-of-Experts architecture and innovative looping mechanism allow it to deliver impressive results without requiring expensive enterprise hardware. It is also designed for fast inference, with additional speed improvements possible through speculative decoding. The best part is that you can run a 4-bit quantized version on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 with 24GB of VRAM. This makes it an interesting option for developers and vibecoders who want a capable local model without depending on paid APIs. In this tutorial, we will run Inkling 2 Mini on an RTX 3090 using Unsloth Studio and put it through a few practical tests. We will generate a financial dashboard, build a playable 2D endless-runner game, and connect the model to the Pi coding agent to see how well it handles real coding tasks. 1. Install Unsloth Studio First, we need to install Unsloth Studio. It provides a simple web interface for downloading, running, and testing AI models locally without dealing with complicated setups. You don't necessarily need an expensive GPU for this. You can use a smaller GPU or even your system RAM, depending on the quantized version of the model you choose. However, for this tutorial, I am using an NVIDIA RTX 3090 with 24GB of VRAM. To get started, open your terminal and run the following command: curl -fsSL https://unsloth.ai/install.sh | sh The installer will automatically detect your system and install the required components. During installation, you might be asked whether you want to start Unsloth Studio immediately. For now, select n , as we need to configure a few things first. Start Unsloth Studio now? [Y/n] n Next, restart your terminal shell so that the newly installed commands are available. exec bash Now, let's configure where our downloaded models and cache files will be stored. AI models can take up quite a lot of space, so it is better to keep everything in one location. For this tutorial, we will store them in a folder inside our home directory. export HF_HOME="$HOME/models/huggingface" export HUGGINGFACE_HUB_CACHE="$HF_HOME/hub" export XDG_CACHE_HOME="$HOME/.cache" You can change these paths depending on where you have free storage. Just make sure you have enough space for the model you plan to download. Finally, start Unsloth Studio using the following command: unsloth studio -H 127.0.0.1 -p 8080 This will start the server on port 8080. On the first launch, you may be asked to create a password to access the interface. Once the server is running, open your browser and visit: http://localhost:8080 You should now see the Unsloth Studio interface, where you can download models, chat with them, and adjust different settings. That's it. We have successfully installed Unsloth Studio. Next, we will download and load Inkling 2 Mini using a 4-bit quantized version that can fit on our RTX 3090. 2. Load and Test Inkling 2 Mini Once Unsloth Studio is running, open the web interface and log in using the password you created earlier. You will see a simple interface where you can chat with models, enable tools, and adjust different settings. To get started, click on the model selection menu and search for Inkling 2 Mini . Select the model, and Unsloth Studio will automatically download and load it for you. For this tutorial, we are using unsloth/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF with the UD-Q4_K_XL quantization, which works well with our RTX 3090. The download might take a few minutes, depending on your internet connection. Once it's done, the model will be loaded automatically, and you can start chatting with it right away. For our first test, we enabled web search and asked the model whether we should buy NVIDIA stock. The model searched the web, gathered information from different sources, and gave us a detailed answer pretty quickly. It was interesting to see a local model handle a research-heavy question so well. We were also getting around 52 tokens per second on average , which is quite impressive for a model running on a single RTX 3090. Next, we wanted to try something more interesting. We asked the model to build an oil market dashboard that tracks different oil prices and indices. For this test, we disabled the tools because we wanted the model to generate the website directly without relying on Python or other tools. The result was surprisingly good. It created a clean dashboard with different oil price indicators, charts, and other useful information. What impressed me most was that the dashboard looked and behaved like a live market dashboard. It simulated price movements and updated the numbers even though the actual markets were closed. Of course, these were simulated values rather than real-time market data, but the overall design and functionality were really good. 3. Connect Inkling 2 Mini to the Pi Coding Agent Now that we have tested the model in Unsloth Studio, let's take things a little further and use it with a coding agent. For this, we will use Pi, a lightweight terminal-based coding assistant that can help us build applications, write code, and work on projects directly from the terminal. First, install Pi using the following command: curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh Once the installation is complete, restart your terminal shell: exec bash -l Next, go back to Unsloth Studio and open the API settings. You will find the connection details and API key needed to connect your local model to Pi. Unsloth also provides a command that makes this process quite simple. Copy the command from your setup and run it in the terminal. For Linux, it should look something like this: export UNSLOTH_STUDIO_URL="http://0.0.0.0:8080" unsloth start pi --api-key YOUR_API_KEY --model unsloth/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_XL Make sure to replace YOUR_API_KEY with your own API key. If Unsloth Studio is running on another machine, use that machine's accessible server address instead. That's it. We can now use Inkling 2 Mini directly from our terminal through the Pi coding agent. To see how well it performs, I decided to give it a more challenging task. I asked it to build a 2D endless-runner game inspired by Subway Surfers, with animations, obstacles, collectible coins, and other visual effects. Here is the prompt I used: Create a fully playable, visually stunning 2D Subway Surfers-style endless runner game using HTML5 Canvas, CSS, and JavaScript, featuring three-lane movement, jumping, sliding, trains, obstacles, collectible coins, power-ups, smooth character animations, parallax scrolling city backgrounds, colorful cartoon graphics, particle explosions, glowing effects, motion blur, speed trails, dynamic lighting, screen shake, realistic shadows, sound effects, background music, increasing difficulty, collision detection, score tracking, responsive keyboard and mobile swipe controls, animated menus, pause and restart functionality, and polished arcade-style gameplay optimized for 60 FPS, using original characters and assets. The model started generating the code, and within a few minutes, we had a playable game that we could open directly in our browser. The result was actually pretty impressive. Compared to the basic 2D game we created earlier, this version looked much better.

title: From Messy to Clean: Taming Real-World CSV Files with pandas read_csv()
abstract: From Messy to Clean: Taming Real-World CSV Files with pandas read_csv() The process of building a bulletproof Python loader based on Pandas' read_csv() function to turn messy data into pristine data. By Iván Palomares Carrascosa , KDnuggets Technical Content Specialist on November 24, 2026 in Data Science Introduction Anyone spending part of their working time in real-world data science may have quickly realized an absolutely harsh truth: pristine, neatly formatted datasets in CSV files are a myth. Real-world datasets, simply put, often look more like a nightmare: from useless metadata placed at the top of the file to rogue semicolons pretending to be the commas that separate features, plus formatting errors. On top of that, enterprise and open dataset files are typically massive, leading to crashes when we try to analyze them in a humbler setting like a Python notebook — all before we even get to view the data. This article shows the process of building a bulletproof Python loader based on the pandas read_csv() function to turn messy data into pristine data. The NYC Airbnb open dataset will serve as a great example of user-generated data chaos. First, we will look at several common issues in CSV file reading one at a time, from a conceptual angle. After that, we will combine the ideas learned into a memory-efficient, reusable loader function that you can easily replicate and adapt to your own datasets and data science notebooks. We will illustrate the practical results of using this unified function on the Airbnb dataset. Tackling Common CSV Reading Issues In smaller hardware settings, RAM limitations are our first enemy when handling large dataset files. Trying to run pd.read_csv() on a 10GB file can easily kill your execution kernel. Therefore, we need defensive strategies such as a parameter called chunksize . It makes read_csv() return an iterator that allows us to process the data in manageable chunks. Let's take a look at the first chunk: import pandas as pd # NYC Airbnb Dataset (~7MB): Messy, user-generated data DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexeygrigorev/datasets/master/AB_NYC_2019.csv" # Prototyping: Reading in chunks of 10,000 rows at a time df_chunks = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL, chunksize=10000) # Pulling the first chunk to see what's inside first_chunk = next(df_chunks) print(f"First chunk shape: {first_chunk.shape}") print(first_chunk.head()) Example output: First chunk shape: (10000, 16) id name host_id \ 0 2539 Clean & quiet apt home by the park 2787 1 2595 Skylit Midtown Castle 2845 2 3647 THE VILLAGE OF HARLEM....NEW YORK ! 4632 3 3831 Cozy Entire Floor of Brownstone 4869 4 5022 Entire Apt: Spacious Studio/Loft by central park 7192 host_name neighbourhood_group neighbourhood latitude longitude \ 0 John Brooklyn Kensington 40.64749 -73.97237 1 Jennifer Manhattan Midtown 40.75362 -73.98377 2 Elisabeth Manhattan Harlem 40.80902 -73.94190 3 LisaRoxanne Brooklyn Clinton Hill 40.68514 -73.95976 4 Laura Manhattan East Harlem 40.79851 -73.94399 room_type price minimum_nights number_of_reviews last_review \ 0 Private room 149 1 9 2018-10-19 1 Entire home/apt 225 1 45 2019-05-21 2 Private room 150 3 0 NaN 3 Entire home/apt 89 1 270 2019-07-05 4 Entire home/apt 80 10 9 2018-11-19 reviews_per_month calculated_host_listings_count availability_365 0 0.21 6 365 1 0.38 2 355 2 NaN 1 365 3 4.64 1 194 4 0.10 1 0 This first glimpse at the data shows it is a bit of a mess, with issues like missing values pervading it all. We will look at a cleaner version of this at the very end, once we build the reusable function based on the conceptual pieces we define next. But first, let's outline several useful patterns to follow for a variety of data cleanliness issues. Junk header rows: real-world data exports generated by widespread tools like SAP and government platforms attach "report metadata" at the beginning of the file, with information such as creation date, author, and so on. pandas can no longer infer the column schema if these lines are not handled properly during loading. Use the skiprows parameter to bypass these unnecessary lines at the start of the file and tell pandas exactly where the true header begins: df = pd.read_csv( DATA_URL, nrows=100, skiprows=0 # NOTE: Change this to 2, 3, etc. if your file has several lines of metadata at the top ) Navigating bad encodings: weird characters like international accents are not unusual, especially in open datasets. pandas can easily end up throwing a fatal UnicodeDecodeError if a byte it cannot decode pops up. If you suspect your data may contain such characters, try using the encoding_errors='replace' option to replace unreadable characters with a placeholder character instead of letting your code crash: df = pd.read_csv( DATA_URL, nrows=100, encoding='utf-8', encoding_errors='replace' # Keeps the kernel alive when hitting bad bytes ) Mixed delimiters: many CSV files are comma-separated, but sometimes there might be semicolons or pipes instead. Handling mixed separators couldn't be easier: pass a regular expression character class like '[...]' that splits on all of them: df = pd.read_csv( DATA_URL, nrows=100, engine='python', # Required for regex separators sep=r'[,;\|]', # Splits on comma, semicolon, or pipe on_bad_lines='skip' # Skips rows that get mangled by the regex ) Thousands separators in large numbers: this is particularly common in statistical and financial datasets, where numbers are stored as strings containing commas, for instance, "1,000,235.00" . To be able to apply math to these values, use the following parameter to handle these separators instantly: df = pd.read_csv( DATA_URL, nrows=100, thousands=',' # Strips commas from numbers automatically ) Parsing mixed date formats: the last trick is invaluable for dealing with inconsistent date formats, where one row uses MM/DD/YYYY , whereas another could be June 29, 2026 . You can parse them immediately upon loading by using date_format='mixed' (available in pandas 2.0 and later): df = pd.read_csv( DATA_URL, nrows=100, parse_dates=['last_review'], # The Airbnb dataset tracks when properties were last reviewed date_format='mixed' # Intelligently handles varying datetime formats ) Bringing It All Together Now it's time to put all these ideas together by combining the defenses we've covered into a robust, reusable function. Use the code below in a Python notebook cell to see how it works on the Airbnb dataset in a matter of seconds: import pandas as pd def load_and_clean_messy_csv(file_url, chunk_size=10000): """ A robust loader for messy, massive CSV files. Yields cleaned pandas DataFrames in manageable chunks. """ print(f"Initializing bulletproof loader for: {file_url}") # Creating the chunk iterator with our defensive parameters chunk_iterator = pd.read_csv( file_url, # 1. Memory management (prevents kernel crashes on huge files) chunksize=chunk_size, low_memory=False, # 2. Bypassing junk (set to 0 here, adjust for SAP/enterprise exports) skiprows=0, # 3. Bad encodings (prevents fatal read errors on emojis/special chars) encoding='utf-8', encoding_errors='replace', # 4. Delimiters (uncomment the line below if your dataset file mixes commas and semicolons, # and remove low_memory=False above, which the python engine doesn't support) # sep=r'[,;\|]', engine='python', # 5. Thousands separators (cleans numeric strings on import) thousands=',', # 6. Mixed date formats (intelligently parses messy date columns) parse_dates=['last_review'], date_format='mixed', # Bonus: Skipping severely corrupted lines that have too many columns on_bad_lines='skip' ) return chunk_iterator # --- Execution --- if __name__ == "__main__": # Lightweight, real-world dataset (loads in ~2 seconds) AIRBNB_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alexeygrigorev/datasets/master/AB_NYC_2019.

title: 7 Most Downloaded AI Models on Hugging Face
abstract: 7 Most Downloaded AI Models on Hugging Face The most downloaded AI models on Hugging Face aren't the ones you'd expect. Discover why smaller, older, and specialized models dominate the rankings. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on November 24, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence You might expect models like Llama , Qwen , DeepSeek , or Mistral to dominate the most-downloaded AI models on Hugging Face . Surprisingly, the list looks very different. Instead of massive language models, we see small embedding models, rerankers, speech recognition systems, and even older models like GPT-2 and BERT. Why? Because downloads don't necessarily reflect which models are the most powerful or popular among AI enthusiasts. They often reflect how frequently models are used in applications, research experiments, automated workflows, and tutorials. Let's explore seven of the most downloaded models on Hugging Face, what they do, and why they remain so popular. 1. all-MiniLM-L6-v2 This lightweight sentence embedding model converts text into 384-dimensional vectors that represent its meaning. It's widely used for semantic search, document similarity, clustering, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Its popularity comes from its simplicity, small size, and efficiency. You can run it on a CPU, integrate it into Python applications, and build useful search systems without needing an expensive GPU. It's also one of the most commonly used models in beginner tutorials, making it a natural choice for developers experimenting with embeddings. Downloads: 182,461,837 2. ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 This cross-encoder model specializes in reranking search results. For example, a search engine might retrieve 20 relevant documents using embeddings. This model then compares each document with the original query and assigns a relevance score to improve the ranking. It's especially useful in RAG pipelines, enterprise search, and question-answering applications. Although it doesn't generate answers like ChatGPT , it helps applications retrieve better information before passing it to a language model. Downloads: 66,397,898 3. bge-small-en-v1.5 Developed by the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI), bge-small-en-v1.5 is a feature extraction model that converts text into 384-dimensional embeddings. These embeddings capture semantic meaning, making the model useful for semantic search, document retrieval, text similarity, and RAG applications. Its popularity comes from its small size, fast inference, and ability to run locally without requiring expensive hardware. It's also widely integrated into vector databases, retrieval frameworks, and AI tutorials. Downloads: 49,421,693 4. MiniMax-H3 Unlike the previous models, MiniMax-H3 focuses on video generation. This particular repository contains model files repackaged for ComfyUI , a popular node-based interface for generative AI workflows. Developers and creators can use these models for text-to-video, image-to-video, and other video-generation workflows. Its presence shows that Hugging Face is not just about language models. Creative AI tools and their supporting model files can also generate significant download activity. Downloads: 31,821,266 5. GPT-2 GPT-2 , released by OpenAI in 2019, might seem outdated compared with today's language models. However, it remains useful for learning, research, benchmarking, and experimenting with text generation. Its relatively small size makes it practical for Google Colab notebooks, educational projects, and experiments involving fine-tuning or language model internals. Many tutorials and research implementations still reference GPT-2, contributing to its continued download activity. Downloads: 29,775,719 6. bert-base-uncased Introduced by Google in 2018, BERT helped transform natural language processing (NLP). Unlike modern chat-oriented generative models, BERT is an encoder model designed to understand and represent text. It's commonly fine-tuned for text classification, named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, and other NLP tasks. BERT remains a standard baseline in research and education, and many applications continue to use its architecture. Downloads: 29,590,515 7. Chronos-2 Chronos-2 is a 120-million-parameter time series forecasting model designed to predict future values from historical data. Unlike traditional language models, it specializes in forecasting patterns in data such as stock prices, electricity demand, retail sales, and weather measurements. It supports univariate and multivariate forecasting, meaning it can predict a single variable or multiple related variables. It can also incorporate additional information, such as holidays or other known future events, to improve its predictions. Its popularity comes from its small size, fast inference, and ability to generate forecasts without task-specific training. Developers can run it locally on CPUs or GPUs, making it useful for research, forecasting experiments, and practical business applications. Downloads: 24,324,549 Why Aren't the Biggest Large Language Models at the Top? There are several reasons why these smaller and older models receive so many downloads. Automatic downloads: When someone runs a tutorial, Google Colab notebook, or application using a Hugging Face model, the required files can be downloaded automatically. Repeated runs across environments can contribute to download counts. Research and education: Models like BERT and GPT-2 are established research baselines. Thousands of tutorials, experiments, and academic projects continue to use them. Production applications: Embedding models and rerankers are used in systems that process large volumes of search queries and documents. They're practical building blocks for everyday AI systems. Lower hardware requirements: Smaller models are easier and cheaper to deploy, making them accessible to developers without powerful GPUs. Automated infrastructure: Continuous integration pipelines, cloud deployments, container builds, and temporary environments can repeatedly fetch the same model. There's another important detail: Hugging Face counts qualifying model-file requests, including certain HTTP GET and HEAD requests. Therefore, download numbers don't represent unique users, complete weight downloads, or actual inference executions. Abid Ali Awan ( @1abidaliawan ) is a certified data scientist professional who loves building machine learning models. Currently, he is focusing on content creation and writing technical blogs on machine learning and data science technologies. Abid holds a Master's degree in technology management and a bachelor's degree in telecommunication engineering. His vision is to build an AI product using a graph neural network for students struggling with mental illness. <= Previous post Next post =>

title: MCP servers can now ship skills, run tasks, and more with Claude
abstract: Skills over MCP is now in public beta in Claude, so MCP servers can ship skills alongside their tools. We're also giving servers ways to handle longer, more interactive work with Claude: Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available, and File Uploads is rolling out soon. Two years ago, Anthropic launched the Model Context Protocol (MCP) as a new standard for connecting AI agents to the systems where data lives. The spec has kept evolving to meet the connectivity needs of agents in production, and is becoming foundational for agentic messaging and orchestration. With today’s updates, Claude can work with a server more like it works with another agent: learning from it, delegating to it, and exchanging input and files along the way. Ship expertise alongside tools with Skills over MCP Tool names and descriptions tell Claude what a server can do, but don't cover how to handle specific use cases. With Skills over MCP , servers can publish skills alongside their tools to help Claude take on longer, multi-step work. Claude loads a skill only when it's needed, keeping context use low. Skills update with the server, so developers can ship tools and guidance together and users have nothing separate to install. Skills can cover best practices, step-by-step workflows, or even playbooks tailored to a user's account or organization. Using Skills over MCP: Shopify helps Claude design and update a merchant's online store end to end. HubSpot onboards customers and gets them set up in Claude. Atlassian helps Claude draw on deep organizational context for insights and work analysis. Carta will help Claude draft and issue equity from an uploaded document (coming soon). Skills over MCP is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code, on by default for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans and available to Team plans once an admin enables it. Coming soon to Enterprise. MCP servers can now take on long-running, interactive work with Claude Agents in production are taking on longer, more consequential jobs. Servers can now support that work by running it in the background, checking in with users, and receiving files from Claude. Hand off long-running work with Tasks . Tool calls used to have to finish before Claude could move on. With Tasks, servers can run operations that take time, or even full agent loops, while Claude keeps working and picks up the result when it's ready. Using Tasks, ZoomInfo runs deeper accounts and contact research that previously took several prompts. Ask for input mid-call with Elicitation . Some actions need a user’s sign-off, like spending money or deleting data. With Elicitation, a server can pause to ask the user for input through a form or link, then continue where it left off. Using Elicitation: Supabase confirms costs before creating a paid project and before running destructive SQL. Railway asks before making potentially destructive changes, like removing a service. GitHub has users enter a repository's name before an agent deletes it. Tasks and Elicitation are now generally available in Claude and Claude Code for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans, and rolling out to Team and Enterprise organizations. Send and receive files with File Uploads . Claude will be able to pass files to MCP servers, not just text. The File Uploads extension sends PDFs, spreadsheets, and images to a server without passing them through the context window. File Uploads is rolling out soon in Claude and Claude Code to Pro, Max, Ultra, and eligible Team and Enterprise plans. Add support to your plugins today These features are part of the open MCP spec and its extensions, so a server that supports them works in any compatible client, not just Claude. To add support, see the docs for Skills over MCP , Tasks , Elicitation , and File Uploads . Built on stronger foundations for connecting agents in production Thanks to contributions from across the AI ecosystem, MCP now sees over 700 million monthly SDK downloads, and there are over 10,000 MCP connectors for Claude. We've worked with the MCP community to improve how MCP works in Claude. Over the past year, it has become: More token efficient: Tool search loads tool definitions only when needed, which can cut the context they use by over 85% in multi-server setups. Easier to scale: The latest MCP spec is stateless and supported across Claude products, making it easier to build servers and maintain their reliability as they grow. Simpler to authorize: The Enterprise Managed Auth extension lets admins authorize supported servers once, so users connect automatically. More interactive: The MCP Apps extension brings full interfaces into Claude, beside the conversation or full screen. Together, these improvements make MCP easier to build on and adopt, and give the standard a strong base to continue evolving for the needs of agents in production. Thank you to the MCP community MCP is an open standard, hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation and shaped by the people who build on it. Two years of progress came from the maintainers, contributors, and developers who wrote the spec, built the SDKs, shipped servers, and added client support. Thank you for making MCP what it is today.

title: Turn artifacts into Mac and Windows apps
abstract: Starting today, you can use Claude artifacts to create, run, and share desktop apps. The "Install as app" feature is rolling out in beta in Claude for Mac and Windows. When an artifact is installed as a Mac or Windows app, it gets its own icon and opens in its own window instead of inside Claude. You can share it with others, and it needs your permission before it can interact with your computer. You choose how much to allow. Each app can use Claude and your connectors, and it updates automatically when the underlying artifact is edited. This simplifies the process for building and maintaining apps for both knowledge workers and developers. Requests the app makes to Claude count toward your plan’s usage limits. Artifacts started out as a work output you’d share, like a chart or a webpage. People now use them as tools for everyday work, like a meeting prep page that regularly pulls from their calendar and email, or a tracker for the orders that need to ship that day. If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention. What installed apps can do Installed apps can send notifications or add items to your menu bar or system tray. You choose permissions for each app, and Team and Enterprise admins can turn app permissions and full access on or off for their organization. People at Anthropic have used these to make: Linnet (opens in new tab) , a full layered image editor Phosphor (opens in new tab) , a file manager that looks made for a movie set Sift (opens in new tab) , which sets up folder rules and uses Claude to keep your stuff organized Tern (opens in new tab) , a terminal with Claude by your side to help and explain Vitals (opens in new tab) , a menu bar and tray app for peeking at your computer’s performance You can see more demo apps made by one of our engineers here (opens in new tab) . Permissions There are three levels of permissions: Default: Installed apps can only do what they’d be able to do in a browser. App permissions: Apps can ask to use common features that Claude can tightly control, like creating always-on-top windows, listening for global shortcuts, or sending notifications. Full computer access: Apps can ask to run programs and read, change, or delete your files without asking each time. Your permission only covers the current version of the app, so Claude asks again after every update, even your own edits. If part of an app comes from another website, that part can change without Claude asking you again. You can only give full access to apps you made or, on Team and Enterprise, apps made by people in your organization. Anthropic doesn’t review apps before you install them, so only give full access to apps you trust. Getting started Describe your app to Claude, try it as an artifact, and then click "Install as app." You don’t have to package or sign it, and it uses your Claude account, so there’s no API key or separate login. Install as app is rolling out in beta on all plans. HIPAA-ready organizations and hybrid deployments can’t use it. It’s on by default for Team, with full access off. On Enterprise, it’s off until an owner turns it on. You need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app. Some artifacts can’t be installed, including Claude Docs, Slides, and Sheets. Update Claude for Mac or Windows, open an artifact you use every day, and choose "Install as app" from the Share menu.

title: How to Run NVIDIA Cosmos 3 on Local AI Devices Using Hugging Face Diffusers
Prepare Market Data for Forecasting with NVIDIA Megatron Core
abstract: Market data arrives as a stream of trades and quotes: every execution, bid, and ask, timestamped to the microsecond. Preparing this data for AI-based market forecasting requires turning price and volume histories into consistent inputs for model training and inference. A common first step is aggregating the data into bars—one row per instrument per time unit—with price, volume, and other statistics. Neural networks can learn patterns from these histories across instruments and forecast horizons. NVIDIA Megatron Core is an open-source library of GPU-optimized components for training transformer models at scale. Megatron-LM is a GitHub repository that combines that library with preconfigured training scripts. A preprocessing script turns intraday market bars into model-ready tensors, and a dataset provider feeds them into Megatron’s distributed training loop. This post shows how to preprocess market-bar data and train a model with Megatron-LM to forecast returns and trading volume across multiple horizons. Forecast returns and trading volume Price and volume remain continuous features. A learned patch embedding turns each group of observations into a model input without converting market values into text. A common data interface supports training a shared forecasting model on histories from many instruments. Each training window belongs to one instrument and includes its identifier, so the model can learn instrument-specific behavior within shared parameters. You can also explore longer contexts, different sampling frequencies, and additional features through the same interface. The example forecasts returns and trading volume at several horizons from the same context. Quantitative researchers can use these outputs to study short-term market behavior, trading activity, or execution timing. Point and interval forecasts address different research questions while using the same input representation. You can change the model architecture, optimizer, or training duration while reusing a prepared dataset. Preprocessing records the patch size, context length, and forecast horizons in the saved metadata, making the data configuration an explicit part of each experiment. A consistent representation also separates the source feed from the model. Data from a new vendor or sampling scheme can follow the same row schema, while the dataset provider supplies the same batch fields. Figure 1 shows the pipeline from market bars to training. Figure 1. Market bars are prepared offline into saved dataset splits. A memory-mapped loader supplies batches to Megatron, with reads shared within each tensor-parallel group From price and volume to model-ready sequences The input is a directory of Parquet files with one row per bar and Symbol, Date, Timestamp, Close, and Volume columns, plus optional numeric feature columns. Bars can come from different vendors and sampling schemes, such as one-minute or sub-minute aggregates of tick data. Keep each instrument’s trading day in one file and the files in chronological order. The script sorts each instrument’s daily observations by timestamp. The script derives within-day log returns and log volumes itself, so the overnight gap never enters the inputs. The preprocessor treats rows as observation steps and leaves gaps unchanged. Align the data upstream if you need a regular time grid. preprocessing.py groups consecutive bars for one instrument on one trading day into patches—the model’s tokens—and slides fixed-length context windows over them. Each patch retains the features of its constituent rows. For example, eight bars per patch and 32 patches per window provide 256 observations in a sequence of 32 model positions. An instrument ID identifies the series, and each patch carries its position within the trading day (Figure 2). Figure 2. Consecutive bars form patches for each instrument and day. Patches retain their input features and session-position indices, then form the model’s context windows Run preprocessing and training Before running the example, see the preprocessing README for environment setup, input-file requirements, configuration options, and output tensor formats. First, preprocess the market bars into training-ready tensors: python examples/financial_timeseries/preprocessing.py \ --data-dir /data/bars --out-dir /data/tensors \ --patch-len 8 --context-len 32 --window-stride 16 \ --time-units-per-day 390 --horizons 1,2,5,15 \ --target-mode cumulative --no-allow-overnight-targets Then, run the Megatron training example with the saved tensors: torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 -m examples.financial_timeseries.pretrain_ts \ --ts-data-path /data/tensors --dataloader-type cyclic \ --num-layers 4 --hidden-size 256 --num-attention-heads 4 \ --seq-length 32 --max-position-embeddings 32 \ --micro-batch-size 64 --global-batch-size 256 --train-iters 2000 \ --lr 3e-4 --min-lr 3e-5 --lr-decay-style cosine --lr-warmup-iters 100 \ --tokenizer-type NullTokenizer --bf16 \ --log-interval 50 --eval-interval 500 --eval-iters 20 \ --save /data/ckpt --save-interval 2000 This small model shows the expected input and output formats. Use it to check that preprocessing, the data loader, target masking, and loss computation work together before substituting your forecasting architecture. You can replace this model while keeping the data layer unchanged. forward_step calls the model with patches (B, L, P, F) , inst_id (B,) , and patch_tod (B, L) . loss_func expects a dictionary with return and volshare tensors of shape (B, L, H) , with one forecast per context position and horizon. Any MegatronModule that takes those three inputs and returns that dictionary can replace it. Defining forecast targets Each window includes future targets for every context position, so one forward pass produces forecasts throughout the context rather than only at the end. A causal forecasting model uses only the history available at each position. Forecast horizons can be defined in observation steps or patches. A point target uses the return and volume at a future step; a cumulative target uses the summed log return and total volume over the interval. Volume targets are represented on a log scale. Figure 3 shows both target definitions for the same context. For regular one-minute bars, a horizon of five observation steps corresponds to five minutes. For event-based data, it counts events. Figure 3. Point targets select a future bar; cumulative targets aggregate the future interval. Targets are constructed at every context position and forecast horizon Efficient data loading for distributed training The data pipeline consists of two stages: preprocessing and data loading. Preprocessing builds the features, patches, windows, and targets offline, then writes them as PyTorch tensor files: train.pt , val.pt , test.pt , and meta.pt . Training reads these saved tensors, keeping Parquet parsing and target construction outside the training loop. Prepare once, reuse across runs During preprocessing, the script handles files in order and uses array operations for regular bar layouts, with a per-instrument path for irregular observations. It computes each instrument’s target sequence once and reuses it across overlapping windows. Temporary memory-mapped arrays hold the completed split tensors before they are saved to disk. The saved metadata records instrument mappings, feature names, patch and context lengths, forecast horizons, and normalization statistics. Model and dataset settings can be checked against the same description before training. Map tensors and share batches The data loader reads the saved splits and supplies batches for training or inference. Validation checks that required keys are present, sample counts align, and the stored context length matches the model. Each worker opens the saved file lazily through memory mapping; fetching a sample copies only its selected rows into private memory.

title: What’s New for Game Developers: AI Animation and RTX Tools
abstract: This month’s NVIDIA game development updates help teams bring new graphics, animation, and local AI capabilities into their engines while balancing image quality, performance, and creative intent. This post covers: Developer lessons from the War Thunder NVIDIA DLSS 5 integration NVIDIA Kimodo animation generation in Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8 updates for RTX Spark, speech recognition, and Vulkan NVIDIA RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 and RTX Path Tracing 1.9 improvements for lighting, integration, and debugging Nsight developer tools updates for Fall of 2026 How Gaijin raised War Thunder ’s realism using NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering In an interview , Gaijin Entertainment shares how it integrated DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering into War Thunder ’s Dagor Engine while preserving the game’s established visual identity. The team explains how it adapted its color management pipeline to evaluate DLSS 5 in sRGB before post-processing and UI, then map the results back to linear HDR, saying “DLSS 5 delivers improved highlights and shadows while introducing a new level of microcontrast that we simply haven’t been able to achieve before. The result is a more natural, lifelike image, with finer detail and a stronger sense of realism.” The team also discusses tuning DLSS 5 against its reference look to preserve vehicle markings, surface wear, and material properties, as well as evaluating image quality and performance separately across air, ground, and naval combat. The interview offers developers practical lessons on balancing lighting and material enhancements with their game’s art direction, with ON/OFF comparisons highlighting rainy, overcast scenes. Read the full War Thunder interview. NVIDIA Kimodo is the first model in Unreal Engine 5.9’s guided animation framework Figure 2. NVIDIA Kimodo generates character motion inside Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview’s Sequencer. Animation courtesy of Epic Games Kimodo brings its animation research into Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview, which introduces a guided animation framework and a set of Sequencer tools that help animators work directly with AI motion-generation models. Kimodo is the first model integrated with it, enabling animators to generate character motion right inside Sequencer. The integration pairs GPU-accelerated motion generation with the familiar timeline editor workflow. Animators can describe a motion with a text prompt, draw a spline path for the character to follow, and set target poses at specific frames. The model generates motion that follows these constraints, so teams decide where characters move and how they pose at key moments, bringing creative control into the animation. Explore the Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview release notes and the Kimodo research project . NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8 expands platform and model support The NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK helps developers integrate NVIDIA ACE on-device. ACE is a suite of AI technologies designed to help middleware and game developers build knowledgeable, actionable, and conversational in-game characters. The SDK supports multiple inference backends across GPU and CPU hardware, giving teams a common interface for running AI alongside game graphics. Version 1.8 focuses on platform support and the inference components used in language and speech workflows. Key updates include: RTX Spark: Hardened platform support for developers building applications Updated inference backends: Newer llama.cpp and whisper.cpp versions Expanded speech recognition: Support for the Parakeet automatic speech recognition (ASR) model through whisper.cpp Vulkan integration: Added support for the Vulkan priority API Additional bug fixes across the SDK. Figure 3. The NvIGI SDK brings core and helper plugins, unified APIs, and local execution together to run NVIDIA ACE AI models on a local PC Explore the NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK . NVIDIA RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 adds sampling improvements and reservoir debugging tools RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 is available on GitHub with updates for developers integrating ReSTIR lighting into their renderers. The release adds new sampling options for ReSTIR DI, adds RTX Spark support, and expands the tools used to inspect lighting reservoirs. Release highlights include: Stratified low-discrepancy sampling for ReSTIR DI spatial resampling A fallback sample feature for ReSTIR DI Enhanced reservoir visualization for direct illumination, global illumination, and path tracing, giving developers more ways to inspect the samples used by each technique RTX Spark support Updated Donut and NVRHI components, along with bug fixes Explore the RTXDI SDK and samples on GitHub . NVIDIA Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0 brings live acceleration structure inspection to D3D12 and Vulkan Figure 4. NVIDIA Real-Time BVH Viewer displays a running scene’s ray tracing geometry in a separate window, with controls for inspecting acceleration structures NVIDIA Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0 is now available on GitHub . The utility shows ray tracing acceleration structures while a game or renderer is running. It helps developers understand TLAS and BLAS contents, validate acceleration structure updates, and debug geometry-related ray tracing issues. The viewer integrates at the graphics API level through Direct3D 12 and Vulkan libraries. Developers send acceleration structure builds, copies, queue submissions, and frame boundaries to the viewer, which displays the results in a separate window. Separate windows with its own camera allows it to inspect TLAS independently from the in-game camera. To inspect an existing title without changing its code, developers can use the included sampler. It attaches the viewer to a running D3D12 or Vulkan process and serves as an integration sample. Release highlights include: Visualization modes for primitive, geometry, instance, and cluster IDs, BLAS addresses, instance masks and flags, and acceleration structure update state Per-pixel trace time heatmaps that show which parts of a scene cost the most to trace Support for various geometry filters: flags, types and ray culling Support for Clustered geometry in D3D12 Vendor-agnostic integration with optional vendor-specific paths, plus builds for Windows x64 and RTX Spark Access the BVH Viewer on github and download the v1.0.0 release . RTX Path Tracing 1.9 adds an introductory sample and SHaRC integration Figure 5. Step 8 of the RTX Path Tracing Intro Sample combines ReSTIR DI, SHaRC, and DLSS Ray Reconstruction in a nighttime café scene NVIDIA RTX Path Tracing 1.9 gives developers a more accessible starting point for adding ray-traced lighting and studying a real-time path tracing pipeline. The intro sample uses a hybrid deferred renderer to introduce lighting features one at a time across nine selectable steps. Developers can progress from image-based lighting and screen-space effects to ReSTIR DI, path-traced indirect lighting, and SHaRC radiance caching. SHaRC is also integrated into the main real-time path tracer and enabled by default, providing additional indirect-lighting information to DLSS Ray Reconstruction. Other updates include: RTX Spark support Performance optimizations including real-time subsampling, overlapping DLSS Ray Reconstruction with the next frame’s path tracing, and GPU-side acceleration-structure instance generation Expanded NEE-AT light sampling support for up to two million lights and clustering of emissive triangles into light levels of detail A new design document describing the real-time path tracing pipeline, plus updated dependencies, fixes, and rendering improvements Read the RTX Path Tracing 1.9 release notes and explore the Intro Sample . RTX Global Illumination 2.9 adds improved diffuse GI sample and SER support Release highlights for NVIDIA RTX Global Illumination 2.

title: Q&A: How Everstone Brings Where Winds Meet to Life with NVIDIA DLSS 5
abstract: Where Winds Meet moves between distant mountain landscapes, bustling streets, and quiet moments with its characters. For Everstone Studio, bringing more realistic lighting and materials to this wuxia world means keeping its aesthetics, recognizable characters, and carefully composed atmosphere intact. The team’s ongoing work with NVIDIA DLSS and Streamline provided a foundation for integrating DLSS 5. Artists and engineers evaluated its lighting and material enhancements against the game’s art direction, balancing visual gains with additional performance overhead. We sat down with art director Muzi Li and engine tech lead Cory Zhou to discuss the studio’s integration approach, preserving character identity, the changes that stood out in Jiangnan, and why developers should account for DLSS 5 early in their rendering budgets. Video 1. Where Winds Meet with DLSS 5 What made DLSS 5 a fit for Where Winds Meet ? The world of Where Winds Meet encompasses landscapes and towns, as well as countless details in how people interact with their surroundings. Players might be gazing into the distance from a mountain one moment, then walking down a bustling street the next. We want these scenes to be more than beautiful; we want players to feel their different weather conditions, times of day, and moods. What attracts us to DLSS 5 is the room it gives us to explore lighting and materials further. It builds on the image already produced by the game engine, using neural rendering to enhance lighting and material details. Our goal isn’t to pursue greater visual impact for its own sake. It’s to make these details work in harmony with the original art direction: distant landscapes should retain their poetic atmosphere, while nearby buildings and characters should have a believable sense of texture. What were your art team’s first thoughts of DLSS 5? Our first impression was that the interplay of light and shadow had gained greater depth. When sunlight falls on buildings, fabrics, and characters, the result feels more than just a sharper image. DLSS 5 identifies and tones down overly bright highlights while bringing out more detail in those areas. It also fills in ambient-light details and subtle highlights in the shadows, and recognizes the properties of materials. How did you integrate DLSS 5 into your pipeline? We have consistently integrated the latest DLSS technologies and kept our NVIDIA Streamline integration up to date. As a result, our rendering pipeline already had strong support for DLSS, providing a solid foundation for adopting DLSS 5. This ongoing investment made the upgrade a natural extension of our existing technology roadmap and helped ensure a smooth integration process. How did artists and engineers use DLSS 5 controls to preserve art direction across characters, materials, and lighting? In any given scene, we look at whether characters remain recognizable, whether materials such as fabric, leather, and metal are still visually distinct, and whether changes in lighting and shadow disrupt the scene’s original mood. NVIDIA provides developers with options for model selection and controls over aspects such as structural and tonal strength. For us, artists and engineers need to communicate and iterate based on what we see on screen. One setting might make the environment more striking, but if faces or the overall color palette drift away from the intended look, we need to find a different balance. We want to strike the right balance between visual gains, performance cost, and player preferences, while giving players choices wherever possible. How did you evaluate DLSS 5 image quality and performance? Our evaluation focuses on three key areas: visual quality, performance overhead, and alignment with the game’s artistic direction. Our testing to date indicates that enabling DLSS 5 introduces additional performance overhead, so we assess that cost alongside the visual improvements it delivers. In developing Where Winds Meet , we have consistently explored different graphics technologies to support a wide range of player preferences. In our internal playtesting, DLSS 5 delivered a distinct visual experience, enhancing the overall presentation of our environments and their sense of immersion. Based on these findings, we plan to give players the option to enable or disable DLSS 5. Our approach to visual tuning will be guided by the art team’s creative vision, including selecting the DLSS 5 model that best matches the intended aesthetic. We also aim to make relevant visual controls available to players wherever possible, allowing them to tailor the image to their preferences. On balance, our evaluation has been positive, taking into account the visual improvements, performance overhead, and flexibility offered to players. How does DLSS 5 affect characters? What matters is whether characters feel more naturally part of the world while retaining their own distinctive presence. For example, when a character walks from sunlight into the shade beneath an eave, changes in lighting and materials can help them feel more naturally grounded in the environment. The way different clothing materials respond to light can also give them a stronger presence. At the same time, we pay close attention to whether faces and costumes remain recognizable. Which scene best demonstrates the improvements? We find that Jiangnan is where DLSS 5 makes the biggest visual improvement. \When adjusting the settings, we use DLSS 5 to soften highlights in the original scene lighting that can appear too harsh, while adding a greater sense of depth between buildings. DLSS 5 can recognize ambient color from the sun and fill in details in darker areas, giving shadows more depth and material detail. Many buildings in Jiangnan feature wood and tiled roofs; DLSS 5 can fill in lifelike wood and roof-tile details. As for the image that best showcases the effect, it will reveal itself during each player’s own journey: perhaps at a street corner just after the rain has cleared, or at an old ferry crossing bathed in the setting sun—a quiet moment that makes you stop and linger. What advice would you give other developers adopting DLSS 5? First, account for DLSS 5 performance requirements early in your rendering budget. For projects targeting high frame rates, reserve sufficient performance headroom and evaluate the balance between visual benefits and performance cost in representative gameplay scenarios. Second, work closely with the NVIDIA team throughout integration and tuning to understand the technology’s capabilities and available controls. Align that work with your project’s artistic direction and performance targets. Resources for game developers See our full list of game developer resources here and follow us to stay up to date with the latest NVIDIA game development news: Follow us on social: X , LinkedIn , Facebook , and YouTube Join our Discord community

title: Introducing the Amazon Bedrock Trusted Access API, with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards and Enterprise Data Controls for Claude models
abstract: Today we are announcing the general availability of the trusted access program API on Amazon Bedrock . The API gives you one place to discover, request, and enroll in model provider trusted access programs. We are also announcing the public preview of the first two offerings for Claude models: Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) and Enterprise Data Controls (EDC). Both are available on Amazon Bedrock, including Claude Fable, Claude Mythos, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 used through the Cyber Verification Program (CVP). Frontier AI labs require stricter safety monitoring policies to their most capable models, and those policies still apply on Amazon Bedrock. For eligible customers, model providers also offer customers more control on how those policies are met, such as where retained data is stored and how it is reviewed. Each offering has its own terms, approvals, and settings. The Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API gives every provider offering one consistent Amazon Bedrock experience. Your teams discover offerings, check eligibility, and enroll in the same way for every provider. Your administrators decide who can enroll, using existing IAM policies and service control policies. As more model providers add offerings, those appear in the same place. EFS and EDC were built in partnership between AWS and Anthropic. They let you access Anthropic’s most capable models safely, from both a model use and a customer data perspective. With both EFS and EDC, when automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for your team to review. With EFS, customers store their data in their own AWS account, and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic or Amazon Bedrock. With EDC, retained data is stored in Amazon-managed storage instead of your account and prompts and completions are not retained by Anthropic. One application gives access to both offerings. In this post, we explain how the trusted access program API works, then walk through EFS and EDC storage options and setup. A trusted access program is a named provider program that gives customers more control of safety reviews and access to model capabilities in exchange for accepting the program’s terms. Amazon Bedrock trusted access program API now gives you one place to find the model and use case programs available to your account. EFS and EDC are the first offerings available today. Offerings that providers add later appear in the same place and follow the same steps. Anyone with access to the trusted access program API can list the offerings and check their status for an account, an organization in AWS Organizations, or an Amazon Bedrock project. The status tells you what to do next. eligible means you’re eligible for the offering and can enroll, requestable means you need approval for eligibility first, and the statusReason field in the response explains how to request it. The model provider (or AWS, as authorized by the model provider) approves your eligibility. Enrolling is a separate step where you accept the offering’s terms imposed by the provider. You enroll at the scope where you were approved: an account, every account in an organization from the management account, or a single project. You can opt out at any time. Each step is a call to the trusted access program API, so you control who can enroll with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and service control policies (SCPs). More information is available in the trusted access programs documentation . With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), you can retain your data in your own AWS environment with full control. It is designed with over 100 customers, including a quarter of the Fortune 100 and many companies in industries with strict rules on data visibility, like healthcare, financial services, and law. Automated safety monitoring looks for patterns that only show up across many requests. These include intentional misuse that could lead to serious harm, such as offensive cyber operations. They also include agents that go beyond what a user asked for, such as using a software exploit to reach an internal system. On Amazon Bedrock, AWS operates EFS and the customer inputs and outputs stay within the customer’s AWS account. Only automated safety monitoring within AWS reads the retained inputs and outputs. AWS human reviewers don’t review content for EFS. Your review stays with you. Neither AWS nor Anthropic humans access your retained inputs or outputs. Your inputs and outputs are never used for training. Amazon Bedrock reaches your AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket as a single AWS service principal and only through the key policy and bucket policy that you write. You can remove that access at any time, but Amazon Bedrock stops serving the covered models 24 hours after it loses access to your key or bucket. When you call a covered model including Claude Fable, Claude Mythos, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 used through the Cyber Verification Program (CVP): A Case summarizes what automated safety monitoring found and references the related transcripts. Retained records arrive under the transcripts/ prefix in your bucket, and case files arrive under review-cases/ . Your team reviews each Case and writes a response file to review-responses/ , stating whether it found a violation ( violation or no_violation ) and, for a violation, the applicable policy category. EDC offers the same automated safety monitoring as EFS and human review of flagged activity stays with your team. Unlike EFS, EDC stores retained data in Amazon managed storage, encrypted with AWS managed keys, so there’s no bucket or key to set up. Eligible customers can access both EFS and EDC through a single enrollment application. If your policy allows retained data to stay in Amazon-managed storage and encrypted with AWS-managed keys, enroll in EDC. If your policy instead requires retained data to be encrypted with your AWS KMS key and stay in your S3 bucket, enroll in EFS. Either way, your team will be able to review flagged activity. Outside EFS and EDC, you can use Claude Fable models on Amazon Bedrock in two ways today: With EFS, retained data is stored only in your own S3 bucket, encrypted with your KMS key. Neither Anthropic nor AWS keeps it in their own storage. The following table compares EFS with the other routes. Table 1: Routes for Claude Fable models on Amazon Bedrock. Storage configurations apply to one Region at a time, and a Region without a configuration uses Amazon-managed storage. Save a configuration in every Region where you call covered models. Start by checking your EFS status with the trusted access program API: If the status is eligible , your account is approved. If it’s requestable , follow the steps in the statusReason field to request access. Joining the preview turns off the interim ZDR exception for the accounts you add. After you’re approved, set up EFS in each Region where you call covered models: The EFS documentation has the complete key policy, bucket policy, IAM policy, and API calls for each step. It also covers organization and project configurations, and troubleshooting. To use enterprise data controls instead, skip steps 1 and 2 and choose Amazon-managed storage in step 3. The trusted access program API, now generally available, gives you one way to find model provider offerings on Amazon Bedrock, check your status, and enroll, with IAM policies and SCPs controlling who can opt in. EFS and EDC are the first offerings in public preview. They give you control over your data when you use Claude Fable and Cyber Verification Program models. With your own Amazon S3 bucket, Amazon Bedrock keeps no copy of the retained data, your AWS KMS key encrypts it, and every access appears in your own AWS CloudTrail logs. To get started, check your EFS status with aws bedrock list-trusted-access-programs and enroll in the EFS preview.

title: Responding to objections to recursive self-improvement
abstract: Okay, so I recently released this essay and this video about recursive self-improvement and why I expect superintelligence by 2030. A wild claim, and understandably, lots of people had objections. Many of them are actually quite interesting and compelling, and I want to go through them here. And by the way, I’m joined by Max Farrens , who is my General Manager, and we ended up discussing all of these ideas as we were writing them down. And in fact, we paired in a lot of the writing. I think a good place to start is with a comment on the Substack version of the post that comes from a user named Jim, who writes as The 1690 Project. “Dwarkesh, do you have a real job where you use this stuff” (meaning AI) “in and day out? I am guessing you do not, because I do, and this is not what I am seeing at all.” What do you think? Those are two different questions. Do I use these things day in, day out? Yes. Do I have a real job? Debatable. Don’t answer that. Funny that the guy’s like bragging about having a real job. He’s like, he’s like a gotcha on me. Like, I’ve been one of the main people who for the last year and a half has been arguing that the basic learning capabilities that these models lack do in fact impair their productivity. I think people who a naive understanding of what it means to automate a job just look at a system like GPT-6 and say, oh, why can’t we have AGI? It can automate all the white-collar work. I think this is totally wrong. The point I’m making in this essay is that are currently worse than humans at almost everything, right? IT is 1% of the economy, well-scoped coding tasks is a small fraction of IT. In some things, AIs are in fact getting to human level or beyond human level, where we have lots of verifiable proxies. And I would argue that just like math, AI research has a lot of verifiable proxies. And so the consequences of narrow progress in AI research or towards AIs that can do AI research leads to general improvements in AI capabilities. So if you look at a system like GPT-3 and you compare it to GPT-6, GPT-6 is also narrow intelligence, right? It can solve Millennium Prize problems, but it can’t be my video editor. So it can do basically everything way better than GPT-3. What I am imagining is that disproportionate progress in ML research, or AIs that are good at doing ML research, will compress as much progress as we had between GPT-3 and GPT-6 into a single year. And so the end result is within a year of having a system like GPT-7 or GPT-8 or whatever it ends up being, we end up with systems that are more generally capable in the way that humans are generally capable, and are on track to then rapidly become better than humans at everything. So Cindy Wu writes on X , “Dwarkesh conveniently sweeps under the rug that climbing a metric involves defining it. Supposing you define it in a way that avoids Goodharting, reward hacking, etc., you need data and environments which do the lifting on defining good metrics. This is most of the game of making AGI, converting fuzzy concepts to formalized objects you can climb without gaming, which requires costly fixes later. He elides the hard problem by saying AI will just automate data.” I think there’s two parts to Cindy’s objection here. One is: can we find metrics which capture general AI progress? Are we aware of such metrics? And two, will we be able to generate the data that makes AIs good at getting better at those metrics? A big part of my essay was dedicated to articulating what those verifiable proxies for general AI progress are, right? So in pre-training, the loss on a held-out corpus is not only a proxy for pre-training progress, it is the basis of pre-training progress, and that is extremely verifiable. And there’s a lot of other proxies you can come up with that are just general intelligence capabilities that are kind of agnostic for any given paradigm. For example, how fast do you master a video game you’ve never seen before? This is one of the key ways that humans are different from current AIs, that humans master new video games really rapidly. How fast can an AI that has only seen a data corpus up to 1700 figure out general relativity? How many open math problems can it solve, right? So there’s a lot of paradigm-agnostic, hard metrics of progress we can come up with. The second argument here is learning algorithms. The application of learning algorithms is very general. The transformer was invented to beat the existing state of the art in translation, but because that architecture, or the implications of the architecture, were general, it also was really good at predicting the next token in WikiText. It’s also really good at generating images and so on. And similarly with reasoning models. Initially they were invented and they were debugged to, like, solve high school math problems and simple coding problems, and now they’re applicable and useful across lots of different domains. And so the breakthroughs that are made in AI end up being measurable on lots of different metrics. And the reason they’re measurable across lots of different metrics is because AI, or intelligence, is general, and because of that, its general improvements show up and make contact with reality in lots of different ways. So you started out by saying that there were two subpoints you wanted to address. The first is around verifiable proxies, and I think I understand that your answer is something of the sort of: it is not just that there are verifiable proxies that we can hill-climb, they are, like, the things themselves that we can work on. And so AI research makes itself particularly amenable to hill climbing. The second is around how we actually get the data to do that sort of work, and that is the part I don’t think I understand. So I’d be curious what your thoughts are. Yeah. So it is true that data is a big part of AI progress. The question is, what is the nature of those data improvements? And it seems to be the case, based on external evidence, that the nature of those improvements are the things that ML researchers who are not experts in any domain other than ML research are able to do. So when you look at how do pre-training data improvements happen, I actually did some research on this. We ended up spending probably on the order of, like, tens to maybe $100,000 of GPUs on this. Hopefully it was worth it just so I can say this one comment, which is, we did this study about, if you look at data corpuses from... Well, this is Jerry Han, by the way, who’s a student at Princeton. And we did the study: if you look at data corpuses from 2019 up till 2026, and then you look at architectures from 2019 till 2026, which explains why we’ve gotten better at pre-training? And we found that actually data explains more of the progress than the architectures. But what we found is that if you look at how that data has gotten better, so that people have released public datasets of pre-training over time, the main improvements are just better methods for filtering data and better methods for coming up with synthetic data. And this is just work that ML researchers are doing on their computers, who are not experts in Shakespeare or quantum mechanics or whatever is in the pre-training corpus. They’re just doing empirical science about, hey, if I filter the data this way instead of that way, will my end model be better at solving math problems? If I make synthetic data this way instead of that way, will my end model be good at doing law or whatever? And so this is just, like, bread-and-butter ML research work. To jump in, just: you mean as opposed to having to hire a bunch of experts in law and then a bunch of experts in banking and a bunch of experts in... to generate a bunch of, like, very sort of specific examples, it is more that these ML researchers, who themselves may know nothing about these domains, can do it alone. Exactly. Now there is a question about: can you automate those ML researchers?

title: 業界首提“端側超節點”，讓端側AI組隊計算：AI效率暴漲270%，不用換晶片或模型
abstract: 業界首提“端側超節點”，讓端側AI組隊計算：AI效率暴漲270%，不用換晶片或模型 衡宇 2026-11-24 14:35:06 來源： 量子位 端側老炮辛米爾，打通物理AI規模化落地之路 衡宇 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 同樣一組晶片、同樣一批模型，只是改變系統組織計算任務的方式，AI的有效任務吞吐量還能提升多少？ 一家長期深耕端側AI基礎設施的中國科技公司實測， 有效吞吐量能提升270% 。 這背後的道理，可以從一座城市的交通系統說起。 汽車的引擎決定單輛車的效能，道路網路和交通排程則決定整座城市的通行能力。即使車輛效能沒有變化，只要最佳化行駛路線與交通排程，也能在現有條件下提升整個交通系統的執行效率。 這個道理放到端側AI領域同樣適用。 隨著AI走進物理世界，智慧攝像頭、機器人、感測器、邊緣計算盒等裝置不斷增加，算力被部署在工廠、園區等不同場景。 它們搭載著不同架構的晶片，執行著各自的模型，卻往往獨立完成計算任務，難以形成跨裝置的協同。 △ 圖片由AI生成 所以晶片夠強還不夠，怎麼讓這些裝置搭夥幹活，也是一門不簡單的學問。 基於在端側AI領域長期積累的軟硬體技術與工程實踐，辛米爾科技在業界率先提出了端側超節點 （Edge SuperPOD） ，為分散的AI裝置搭建一套協同“路網” 辛米爾告訴量子位： 改變計算任務的組織方式，正在成為釋放端側算力潛力的新路徑。 四散的端側AI算力，和必須直面的三道坎 過去幾年，雲端AI的算力競爭，已經 從單顆晶片的效能比拼逐漸延伸到系統級協同 。 隨著模型規模和計算需求不斷增長，越來越多的GPU被組織成超節點，通過高速互聯和平行計算，共同承擔大規模訓練與推理任務。 如今，類似的計算需求也開始出現在物理世界，只是端側的情況要複雜得多。 智慧相機、機器人、感測器、邊緣計算盒等裝置，分佈在現實世界的不同場景，各自執行著不同的模型，晶片架構與效能參差不齊。 想要它們真正協同起來，首先要跨過三道難關。 第一道是算力分散，資源利用不均。 不同裝置各自執行模型，缺少統一的任務編排機制，容易出現部分GPU閒置、部分NPU滿載的情況。不同模型還可能重複執行相同的預處理，原始資料在裝置間來回傳輸，大量資源消耗在重複計算和資料交換上。 △ 圖片由AI生成 第二道是感知資訊割裂。 相機採集目標外觀資訊，三維感測器提供空間幾何資料，音訊與裝置狀態訊號記錄現場動態。不同感知單元只能獲取場景的一部分，彼此之間缺少有效的資訊整合機制。 想要融合多源訊號，形成完整的場景認知，就需要打破裝置與模型之間的隔離邊界。 第三道是任務部署複雜。 一個完整的物理AI任務往往需要組合多種感測器、模型和計算裝置，而不同晶片架構與開發生態差異明顯。僅演算法適配、資料整合和系統整合，就需要投入大量工程資源。 這三道難題彼此交織。裝置規模越大，任務邏輯越複雜，系統層面的組織與排程就越關鍵。 辛米爾敏銳地看到了這片尚未充分釋放的算力空間。 不同裝置各有所長，如果能圍繞同一個AI任務分工協作，原本零散的感知能力與計算資源，就有機會凝聚成一個整體。 端側超節點，把分散算力組織成一支隊伍 端側超節點的構想由此誕生。 作為辛米爾端側AI基礎設施向系統級協同計算的進一步演進，這套方案跳出了單臺裝置的計算侷限，讓散佈在物理場景中的異構裝置協同聯動，以一個統一系統的形態共同承接AI任務。 眾所周知，雲端AI已經走過了單純比拼晶片效能的階段。隨著計算需求不斷增長，如何將大量GPU組織起來讓它們協同完成任務逐漸成為新的競爭焦點。 辛米爾想把這套系統級計算思路帶到端側。 只是，物理世界遠比資料中心複雜。 雲端超節點 依託相對集中的計算資源和高速互聯，重點解決大規模算力的聚合與排程。 端側超節點 面對的則是分佈在不同位置、採用不同晶片架構的裝置，需要同時處理感知資訊融合、異構算力排程和跨裝置通訊。 要讓這樣一支隊伍真正配合起來，辛米爾圍繞三個環節展開了技術佈局。 其一，感知融合。 傳統方案中，相機看到的是畫面，三維感測器捕捉的是空間，音訊裝置記錄的是聲音。不同裝置各自採集資料、執行模型，再將結果交給上層系統整合。 辛米爾嘗試通過跨模態特徵編碼、時空關聯和統一場景表徵，讓不同感知節點採集的視覺、三維、音訊等資訊進入同一個任務上下文。 原本各自獨立的感知結果，由此有機會形成更完整的場景理解。 與此同時，系統還可以根據任務需要，在節點之間交換結構化事件、特徵或緊湊的多模態Token，減少完整影片、點雲等原始資料的重複傳輸。 △ 圖片由AI生成 其二，彈性排程。 一項複雜的物理AI任務，往往包含許多計算環節。哪些環節需要毫秒級響應，哪些需要更強的推理能力，哪些又可以交給低功耗裝置完成，都需要根據具體任務安排。 辛米爾將複雜任務拆解為具有依賴關係的計算圖，再綜合裝置資源、即時負載、資料位置和通訊成本，動態決定各個計算環節由誰執行。 例如，低功耗NPU可以負責高頻感知和即時判斷，CPU處理通訊與業務邏輯，GPU承擔複雜多模態理解。更高算力的節點則可以按需參與任務規劃、大模型推理與學習最佳化。 不同晶片由此各司其職，不必讓所有任務都擠在少數高效能裝置上。 其三，異構互聯。 裝置之間有了分工，還需要通訊機制來支撐協作。 從晶片內部連線、板級匯流排，到裝置之間的乙太網路，不同通訊鏈路的頻寬和延遲差異很大。簡單地將裝置接入同一個網路，並不意味著它們就能順暢地進行分散式AI計算。 為此，辛米爾正在構建統一的跨節點任務通訊與資料交換機制，根據任務依賴、資料位置和網路條件，決定哪些計算留在本地，哪些結果需要傳遞給其他節點，以及何時呼叫更高效能的計算資源。 感知融合、彈性排程、異構互聯，三個環節共同構成了端側超節點的協同計算體系。 其效果最終體現為有效任務吞吐量的變化。 在相同硬體、相同模型條件下，辛米爾通過系統最佳化，實現了有效任務吞吐量提升270%—— 這意味著端側AI的效能潛力還有晶片和模型之外的釋放空間。 通過重新組織感知資訊與計算任務、協調裝置間協作，已有硬體資源也能承擔更多有效任務。 算力組隊之後，端側AI還要過工程關 儘管算力協同解決了裝置如何共同完成任務的問題，物理AI規模化部署仍面臨模型適配成本高、場景變化後需要重新訓練和除錯等挑戰。 物理環境和任務需求不斷變化，專用模型往往需要針對新的裝置和場景重新採集資料、標註、訓練與適配。 對於需要進入大量真實場景的物理AI來說，這類重複工程投入也會逐漸成為規模化部署的成本負擔。 要減少這些投入，光有協同計算架構不夠，還需要把硬體適配、模型執行和裝置管理等能力沉澱到一套可複用的產品體系裡。 為此， 辛米爾圍繞硬體與軟體構建了一套產品體系。 硬體方面 ，公司將不同梯度的AI算力與視覺、3D、紅外、音訊等感知能力進行模組化組合，形成從即時感算終端、多模態協同終端到高算力工作站的產品矩陣。 不同場景可以根據任務需求，選擇相應的算力與感知模組。 軟體方面， 端側AI作業系統EdgeFlowOS負責打通不同晶片與裝置，提供模型執行、任務編排、跨節點協同及統一管理等能力，並通過標準化的軟體介面與部署工具，降低不同場景下的系統適配與整合成本。 經過長期的技術研發與產業實踐，辛米爾已形成覆蓋200餘種晶片平臺、100餘種通用與專用模型的適配積累。 依託橫跨大模型預訓練、晶片架構設計和自動駕駛等領域的研發團隊，公司構建了貫穿模型、算力、軟體與裝置的全棧技術能力。 這些跨平臺、跨模型的技術與工程積累，也為端側超節點的構建及規模化部署奠定了基礎。 說一千道一萬，物理AI真正走向規模化，最終還要算一筆工程賬。 晶片、模型和感測器的能力不斷提升，如果每進入一個新場景，都需要重新完成硬體適配、模型部署和系統整合，技術進步就很難轉化為規模化應用。 隨著異構裝置協同能力和軟硬體適配體系逐漸成熟， 更多能力可以沉澱下來，在新的場景中繼續複用。 這就是端側超節點更長遠的價值所在。 單點能力終有邊界。越來越多的裝置擁有感知和計算能力，物理世界正悄然變成一張巨大的智慧網路。 不同裝置的感知彼此交融，算力協同排程，原本分散的智慧便有機會匯聚成更大的整體能力。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 端側AI 端側超節點 辛米爾科技 衡宇
