title: [AINews] Jensen Is Back! and OpenAI Shows Its Pretraining Curve, joined by Microsoft
abstract: Congrats to Sierra on tripling last year’s $10B valuation , and to Z.ai for releasing GLM 5.4 , their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller Inkling Mini 2 from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories… Jensen Huang is back . Eleven days after announcing his resignation , Nvidia announced his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors. The board voted unanimously after more meetings with Jensen on Sunday and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka the Treasury Secretary and the President dialing into the board meeting ). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control. As Matt Levine points out , with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light. OpenAI put its pretraining loss curve on the record. In Perplexity and Intelligence , Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki plotted base-model log-perplexity back to GPT-3.5 (on their internal held-out coding dataset … which has notable caveats ): Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. Lower is better. GPT-3.5 was around 0.99 and GPT-4 around 0.91. When OpenAI put a model around 0.76 (GPT6 Astra) to work on open math problems, hundreds of frontier math problems started falling quickly . Pachocki extrapolates that another jump in capabilities could come around 0.68–0.70. This is all in context of pacing the frontier . Pachocki proposes that labs agree on a first limit to development and spell out what would let them cross it, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitoring. Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman gave the first win by cosigning and joining in, running MAI-2 Base on OpenAI’s evaluation set and reporting 0.819. We’d need at least a couple more top labs to join this effort for it to gather steam as a real self-regulatory limit, most notably of course, Anthropic. Sponsored by Backblaze B2 If your data is growing faster than planned, you need storage that grows with your business, feeds flash and GPUs with terabit-scale throughput, and doesn’t charge egress. Backblaze B2 has delivered capacity tier storage for twenty years, manages more than six exabytes, and is trusted by leading neoclouds, labs, and gen AI companies. Growth shouldn’t be something you sweat. We’ve got room for whatever you’re building. OpenAI Publishes Its Pretraining Perplexity History and Proposes Shared Development Limits The disclosure : Jakub Pachocki's essay "Perplexity and Intelligence" publishes five years of OpenAI base-model log-perplexity on a fixed held-out dataset. It argues for industry-wide limits based on perplexity and other measurements, with further progress gated on milestones in understanding and monitoring AI behavior, such as a successor to chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors ( essay thread ). Policy framing : Sam Altman quoted the proposal for a first common limit with concrete exit criteria ( quote ). He tied it to the standards commitments in the White House Accords ( accords ). Endorsements : Greg Brockman highlighted the warning that alignment progress is unlikely to keep pace with pretraining acceleration ( gdb ). Mark Chen called the numbers formerly "sensitive IP" and asked other labs to disclose their key metrics ( markchen90 ). Claimed findings : Losses below 0.8 coincided with emergent capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics ( excerpt ). Thresholds and timing : OpenAI expects further "transformative capabilities" in the ~0.68–0.7 window and describes a steep acceleration in 2026 ( summary ). Internal model : An unreleased internal model already sits below GPT-6.2 Astra. Pachocki says pretraining could see an "avalanche" like the recent one in math as soon as 2027 ( scaling01 ). Community extrapolations (unofficial) : Dan Hendrycks infers ~3–5×/yr compute-efficiency gains since GPT-4, possibly 100×+ this year ( hendrycks ). One fit, using the internal model at 0.732 against 0.761 for the released model, reaches 0.70 between January and March 2027 ( fits ). Microsoft joins : With OpenAI's permission, Microsoft AI reported MAI-2 Base at 0.819 on OpenAI's eval set. It shares OpenAI's tokenizer and lands in GPT-5.6 Sol base-model territory. Mustafa Suleyman suggested bits-per-byte for future cross-lab comparisons ( mustafasuleyman ). Open-model mapping : Elie Bakouch used MAI as a bridge to place open models on OpenAI's curve ( plot ). He labels the further chaining through Inkling bpb a "very weak approximation" ( details ). Lucas Beyer's caveat : Inkling's held-out codebase may be largely agent-generated, which would make bridge-based placements look too optimistic ( giffmana ). Methodological critiques : Critics raised several confounds: Tokenizer bias : Common limits could favor OpenAI over Anthropic because of tokenizer differences ( davidmanheim ). Post-training compute : Post-training likely accounts for more than 75% of FLOPs, so pretraining perplexity may be the wrong pacing metric ( stochasticchasm ). Synthetic data : Part of the steep curve may come from a growing share of model-generated pretraining data ( Azaliamirh ). Missing context : Without model sizes or compute figures, it is hard to separate scaling from algorithmic progress ( Grad62304977 ). OpenAI's response : Staff say the eval is fixed over time and excludes model-generated code ( johnohallman ). Will Depue added that it is "held out, frozen, tokenizer agnostic" ( willdepue ). Pressure on other labs : Several researchers asked OpenAI to release the held-out set ( oneill_c ; DimitrisPapail ). Anthropic's redactions : Anthropic redacted pretraining metrics from its METR report ( eliebakouch ), prompting calls to publish them ( _NathanCalvin ). Third-party verification : METR offered to verify pause or compute-allocation claims under its standard terms ( ChrisPainterYup ). Frontier Model and Product Launches: Gemini 4 Neon, GPT-6.2 Sol, Claude Ship Gemini 4 Neon : Google positions Neon between Carbon (hardest long-horizon work) and Hydrogen (fast execution), aimed at complex coding and enterprise workflows ( Google ). Leaderboard results : Neon claims several top spots: LiveBench 2.0 : #1 at 87.4, versus 84.9 for both Claude Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra, at roughly a quarter of Fable's cost per task ( LiveBench ). AI Chess Leaderboard : #1 at 1924 Elo ( chess ). Arena text : Google holds the top three, with Carbon at 1527, Argon at 1520 and Neon at 1513 ( Arena ). Adoption signals : OpenRouter spend on Google models exceeded OpenAI's for the first time since June ( OpenRouter ). Perplexity traffic : Neon is compounding +10.6%/day in Ask and +15%/day in Computer. Aravind Srinivas says this is organic switching from Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.2, not default routing ( growth ; clarification ). Access rules : Gemini subscriptions work only through the Antigravity binary. T3 Code is allowed because it wraps Antigravity; shims such as Pi are not ( theo ; Google confirmation ). Quota changes : Antigravity quotas were reset. Pro users get Carbon, and Hydrogen opens to all users ( _mohansolo ). Workspace : Neon is rolling out to Workspace customers in the Gemini app ( OfficialLoganK ). Hydrogen pricing : Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens. It scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, against 50 for Argon, and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 ( dl_weekly ). API features : New file slicing lets agents upload once and pay only for the pages, cells or clips Gemini inspects ( googledevs ). Function results can now return documents, audio and video natively ( _philschmid ).

title: superdesigndev/treg
abstract:
Treg (OpenRouter for Tools) OpenRouter, but for agent tools instead of models. Point an agent at one base URL with one token
and it can do the job: a curated catalog of thousands of endpoints across many providers — SEO and backlinks,
social and trends, people and company enrichment, ads, scraping, image and video generation — priced per call, from a cent ,
with no provider signup. Plus your own team's keys, skills and CLIs, callable by every teammate's
agent without the credential ever leaving the server. Ask for the task, not the tool. You do not need to know which vendor sells backlink data, or to
hold an account with them. Search for what you want to do, read the price, call it. Built for the Superdesign team, live at treg.to — anyone can self-host. Why it exists The tools an agent needs for real work sit behind subscriptions nobody buys for a single run —
Semrush $139/mo, Moz $99/mo, Crunchbase $99/mo, Apollo $59/seat — behind signup walls, or behind no
public API at all (invite-only, partner-only, app-review-only). treg carries those accounts and
bills fractions of a cent per call. Two kinds of tool, one token The catalog — external endpoints treg can serve with its own key or through a verified public
route that needs no provider key. Own-key calls use the team's prepaid balance; anonymous calls
are free. No account with the provider is needed. New verified accounts receive $1.00 free once, when they create an eligible team. Your own tools — anything a teammate registered: a paid API account, an OAuth connection, a
vendor CLI, a SKILL.md . Your own key always wins over treg's, and those calls are never
metered. The vocabulary for the second half: tool = something the registry calls for you with the org's credential. Two kinds: endpoint — an upstream base_url + credential bindings (each binding injects one
secret into the request; a request can carry several, e.g. an OAuth bearer and a developer-token header). CLI — a vendor binary ( stripe , gh , vercel , ...) run with the credential injected. skill / bundle = a recipe ( SKILL.md ) + its secrets + its tool(s), registered together. The one rule: the proxy relays, never models the upstream, and injects auth server-side — so it survives upstream API changes and callers never hold keys. Part 1 · Using the registry Visit treg.to (hosted on Render) — the dashboard,
sign-in, and every URL below live there. Quickstart Same flow as the dashboard's Getting started guide: # 1. install the CLI — also points it at the registry curl -fsSL https://treg.to/install.sh | sh # 2. sign in (GitHub default · --email for a one-time code · --token for agents/CI) treg login # 3. do something useful immediately — no key, nothing registered treg catalog search " backlinks for a domain " # find a tool by what it DOES treg call tikhub.tiktok.user.profile --query uniqueId=tiktok
treg balance # exactly what that cost # (or `treg onboard` for the guided walkthrough) Fish Audio provides S2.1 Pro speech, public-voice discovery, and private voice cloning.
Speech is binary stdout, so redirect it to a file. A discovered voice's _id or a team voice id is
the TTS reference_id ; voices created on treg's Fish account are durable team resources: treg call fishaudio.tts.s2-1-pro --method POST --header model=s2.1-pro \
  --data ' {"text":"Hello from treg","format":"mp3"} ' > speech.mp3
treg call fishaudio.voices.discover --query self=false --query licensed=false --query language=en
treg resources list --provider fishaudio --kind voice With your own Fish key, requests are an unmetered upstream relay and Fish owns the account boundary. A client written for a provider's own API can switch by its base URL alone: https://treg.to/call/<provider> in place of the provider's base URL ( https://api.dataforseo.com/v3 → https://treg.to/call/dataforseo ) runs the catalog tool on that method and path exactly as /call/<id> would; a path the catalog does not list is a 404, never relayed. Catalog tool inputs are described by treg catalog get <id> . Tools marked strict_query reject undeclared or repeated query parameters, unsupported values and request bodies. Send each declared parameter within its declared type, allowed values and range, each single-valued one once, and a row count such as limit as a whole number within its stated maximum: a tool that enforces this answers a 400 catalog_parameter_invalid naming the parameter, and nothing is charged. Undeclared fields are forwarded as sent. Your token identifies you on every call ( X-Treg-Token header) and is the same for all tools.
Discover what your team has shared: treg tool ls · check credential health: treg health . Or install it as a Claude Code plugin /plugin marketplace add superdesigndev/treg
/plugin install treg@treg Installs the treg skill and treg's tools with no token and no configuration. Run /mcp , pick
treg and sign in; the tools appear after it. Other agents: npx skills add superdesigndev/treg -s treg (or see Workflow skills for the rest).
See docs/CLAUDE-PLUGIN.md . MiniMax Code / MiniMax Agent users: the same
skill ships via the MiniMax Plugin Marketplace ( docs/MINIMAX-PLUGIN.md ). Workflow skills Ready-made recipes your agent runs end to end, every call through treg: Skill What your agent can do treg Find and call any tool in the catalog, plus your own tools web-access When your agent's own web tools fall short, read the live web without local scrapers: free search and page reads first, then the right platform job for social, stores, reviews, maps and papers, with treg falling back to the next vendor when one fails lead-signals Find in-market buyers from public signals (complaints, job changes, hiring, funding, tool adoption) and monitor a topic, competitor or account list for them ( treg.to/leads-signals ) recruit Turn a LinkedIn job post into a ranked shortlist: criteria from the post, people search, filters with reasons, one line on why each fits, cited evidence (posts, GitHub, talks, tenure, job change) under a per-candidate spend cap, then a checked personal email and phone, with a run file of counts, evidence and the vendor trail per candidate doomscroll Catch up on any topic over the last hours: the best posts, clips and reactions from X, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt, grouped into stories with links, only what is new since the last scroll make-ugc Make AI UGC videos: trending hooks, a presenter, talking-head clips, captions ( treg.to/ugc ) jev-memory Give Claude Code a memory: a Claude Code mod where Jev judges each prompt after the turn and keeps your lasting preferences, installed ready-made or built from one prompt ( the mod ) install.sh installs only treg and names the others in one line; your agent offers them after
sign-in and the first call. Name the ones you want with sh -s -- --skills lead-signals,recruit (or --skills all ; the opt-in jev-memory and rea-growth are never in that set). In Claude Code each one is
also its own plugin in treg's marketplace: /plugin install recruit@treg , or pick them from /plugin . To add
them to an existing agent instead ( skills.sh CLI): npx skills add superdesigndev/treg # every public skill npx skills add superdesigndev/treg --skill lead-signals # just one treg skill bootstrap --skills all # the installer's set, with the treg CLI you already have The workflow skills run on treg, so set it up first (the Quickstart above, or point your agent at treg.to/llms.txt ). Claude.ai connector The Claude Connectors Directory surface is https://treg.to/mcp/v2/ . It exposes only curated
catalog endpoints, without image, video or audio generation, and separates read calls from write
calls so Claude receives accurate safety signals. The existing /mcp/ surface remains available for catalog endpoints, team-owned tools,
and imported skills. See the MCP and OAuth architecture for the boundary and implementation, and the submission runbook for release gates.

title: google-research/paper-orchestra
abstract:
🎻 PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing Yiwen Song 1 , Yale Song 1 , Tomas Pfister 1 , and Jinsung Yoon 1 1 Google Cloud AI Research PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing. It flexibly transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials (ideas and experimental logs) into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including comprehensive literature synthesis and generated visuals, such as plots and conceptual diagrams. Acting like an orchestrated team of specialized agents, it handles outline generation, literature review, section writing, content refinement, and plotting to close the gap between raw research materials and submission ready papers. Key Features Multi-Agent Pipeline : Orchestrates specialized agents (Outline, Literature Review, Section Writing, Content Refinement, Plotting) for end-to-end paper generation. Comprehensive Literature Synthesis : Automatically searches, prioritizes, and integrates relevant literature into the manuscript. Visuals Generation : Generates plots and supports the inclusion of conceptual diagrams. LaTeX Automation : Produces submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts adhering to target conference templates. Installation Environment Setup : The project relies on a Conda environment named paper_orchestra . You can set up a similar environment with Python 3.11 and install the required dependencies. conda create -n paper_orchestra python=3.11
conda activate paper_orchestra
pip install -r requirements.txt Environment Variables : Create a .env file in the root of the project and add your API keys: # Add keys if you have them, otherwise leave them empty # You need to specify related keys if you want to use the model # For example, if you want to use Gemini models, you need to specify either VERTEX_AI_PROJECT and VERTEX_AI_LOCATION, or GEMINI_API_KEY # If you want to use OpenAI models, you need to specify OPENAI_API_KEY SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY = your_semantic_scholar_api_key OPENAI_API_KEY = your_openai_api_key VERTEX_AI_PROJECT = your_vertex_ai_project VERTEX_AI_LOCATION = your_vertex_ai_location GEMINI_API_KEY = your_gemini_api_key # if you want to run demo and send emails to yourself at the end, set these 2 fields as well SMTP_EMAIL = your_email SMTP_PASSWORD = your_password Dataset The dataset used for paper generation is not included in this code repository. It will be released separately at a later date.
Once available, you should download the dataset and place it under the datasets/ directory. Usage You can run the paper generation pipeline using the provided bash script or directly via the Python CLI. Using the Bash Script ./paper_writing_cli.sh Using the Python CLI directly python paper_writing_cli.py \
  --raw_materials_dir /path_to_your_raw_materials/ \
  --latex_template_dir /path_to_your_latex_template/ \
  --output_dir /path_to_your_output_folder/ \
  --use_plotting true Key Arguments --raw_materials_dir : (Required) Directory containing the raw materials (e.g., idea and experimental log). --latex_template_dir : (Required) Directory containing the LaTeX template (e.g., templates/cvpr2025 ). --output_dir : Directory to output the generated paper. If not specified, an automatic folder with a timestamp is created. --use_plotting : Enable the plotting agent workflow to generate figures from code (Default: False ). --writer_model_name : LLM for writer and literature agents. --reflection_model_name : LLM for reflection agents. Interactive Demo We provide an interactive Streamlit demo for the paper generation pipeline. For instructions on how to run and use it, please refer to the README.md in the frontend directory. Project Structure autoraters/ : Contains scripts for automated evaluation. methods/ : Core logic for agents and pipeline execution. templates/ : LaTeX templates for target conferences, you can add your own template by creating a new subfolder under this directory. utils/ : Utility functions for API calls, PDF handling, etc. Citation If you find this repo or our paper helpful, please cite it as follows: @article { song2026paperorchestra , title = { PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing } , author = { Song, Yiwen and Song, Yale and Pfister, Tomas and Yoon, Jinsung } , journal = { arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.05018 } , year = { 2026 } } Disclaimer This is not an officially supported Google product.

title: hieunc229/mailflare
abstract:
Mailflare A self-hosted alternative to Google Workspace. Setup custom domain Emails , Calendar, Drive, Booking and built-in AI agents . Self-host it on Cloudflare or Docker. Or try Mailflare Cloud with high-deliverable emails from $4​ Screenshots Inbox Domains Mailboxes Calendar Booking Drive Features Apps Email : Custom domain mailboxes, personal or shared, with access you control. Send and receive with Cloudflare Email, Resend or Amazon SES. Routing rules : Store, forward, reject or sort incoming mail, including a one-rule filter for newsletters and promotions. Calendar : Repeating events with time zones. Attendees get email invitations. Booking : Share a public link so anyone can book a free time on your calendar. Drive : Store and share files. AI agents : Search mail, draft replies and manage events. Connect other AI tools over MCP. Technical Databases : Cloudflare D1 (default), PostgreSQL, MySQL, Turso / libSQL, or a local SQLite file. Set DATABASE_URL to switch. Works with Supabase, Neon, PlanetScale, TiDB and more. See Databases . File storage : Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2 or AWS S3. Hosting : Cloudflare Workers or a single Docker container. Admin : Users, API keys, webhooks, audit logs and backups. Import : Bring in mail from IMAP, Gmail Takeout, .eml and .mbox files, and Google Calendar events, Google Contacts and Google Drive files from Takeout. See Importing from Google Takeout . Mailflare currently supports 34 languages, including English, Português (Brasil), Português (Portugal), Español, Français, Deutsch, Italiano, Nederlands, Polski, Українська, Русский, Türkçe, 中文（簡體）, 日本語, 한국어, Bahasa Indonesia, Bahasa Melayu, Tiếng Việt, ไทย, हिन्दी, বাংলা, मराठी, తెలుగు, தமிழ், ગુજરાતી, ಕನ್ನಡ, മലയാളം, ਪੰਜਾਬੀ, සිංහල, Kiswahili, Hausa, plus العربية, اردو and فارسی (right-to-left). Cost You can receive and send mail for free. Receiving : Cloudflare Email Routing is free. Sending : Use the free tier of Resend (3,000 emails a month) or Amazon SES. Cloudflare's own sending needs the $5/month Paid Worker plan. New Amazon SES accounts start in a sandbox. Ask AWS for production access to lift it. Prices change, so check Resend , Amazon SES and Cloudflare . Deploy Deploy the app. Click Deploy to Cloudflare . Keep the app name mailflare , or it will break. Finish setup. Open the app at /setup and create your admin account. Connect a domain. Add a domain from the same Cloudflare account, then create your first mailbox. CF_TOKEN is required. Create a scoped Cloudflare API token with these permissions: All accounts: Email Sending:Edit, DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Addresses:Edit All zones: DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Rules:Edit, Zone Settings:Edit, DNS:Edit More options: deployment guide . Deploy with an AI agent Paste this into an AI agent that has terminal access (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and similar): Install Mailflare for me from https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare on my Cloudflare account.

1. Read README.md, docs/deployment.md and wrangler.jsonc first.
2. Ask me for my Cloudflare account ID and two API tokens, using a secret input:
   a deploy token (for Wrangler) and a runtime token (the Worker secret CF_TOKEN).
   Never print them, commit them, or pass them as command arguments.
3. Keep the Worker name exactly "mailflare". Create or reuse the D1 database
   "mailflare", the R2 bucket "mailflare-raw", and the queues "mailflare-inbound",
   "mailflare-outbound" and "mailflare-agent".
4. Install dependencies, run `npm run deploy`, and set CF_TOKEN as a Worker secret.
   Do not run remote database migrations yourself. The /setup page does that.
5. Give me the app URL and anything I still need to do. I will open /setup, create
   the admin account and connect my domain. Token permissions and more options: deployment guide . Self-host with Docker Runs as one container on any server, with SQLite and local files. cp .env.docker.example .env.docker
docker compose up -d --build Or skip the build and run the prebuilt image: docker compose -f docker-compose.image.yml up -d . See self-hosting . Local development cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars
npm install
npm run db:migrate:local
npm run dev Add your Cloudflare credentials to .dev.vars , then open localhost:3000 . Run npm run db:seed to load sample data. npm run build : build the Worker npm run deploy : build and deploy npm run lint : lint and type check A schema change needs a migration for each database type. See Databases . Documentation Deployment and configuration Databases Sending and receiving providers API and integrations Email assistant and MCP Importing from Google Takeout Adding a language Troubleshooting License See LICENSE .

title: Tidal bans AI-generated music
abstract:
Nov 24, 2026 7:06am PT Tidal Bans AI-Generated Music Tidal The music streaming service Tidal said Tuesday that it would ban tracks it believes are completely AI-generated starting next month, a move its leader believes “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.” The service will remove the AI tracks starting Dec. 9, making Tidal the first music streaming platform to ban AI music entirely. It comes nearly five months after Tidal said it would demonetize any AI-powered song, force those artists to label their tracks as either AI-generated or AI-assisted and ban AI songs that were associated with “fraudulent activity,” a category that includes songs impersonating established artists and efforts to “deceive listeners.” “But that’s enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done,” wrote Robert Andersen, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, in an X thread on Tuesday. “We’ll begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from our catalog, and you’ll see them completely gone by the beginning of the year.” Andersen said that 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays. The move will cleave the platform of 29 million tracks, he added, and have it reject between 80,000 to 85,000 songs a day. “We encourage our peers to follow suit,” he wrote. The move comes as competitors such as Spotify and Apple Music continue to test approaches to combat the rise of AI-generated tracks proliferating on their platforms, many of which the services have labeled some version of “slop” or “spam.” Apple Music said it would also begin labeling AI-generated or AI-assisted tracks on its platform, while Spotify said it would label artists it deemed AI creations as an “AI Persona.” Spotify said in a blog post last month it also removed 50 million slop or spam tracks from users’ recommendations this year, which came after it removed 75 million of those songs from its catalog entirely. The revelation came among a number of updates regarding Spotify’s efforts to combat AI spam. “This work isn’t finished,” Spotify added. “AI moves fast, and bad actors adapt just as fast. But as AI makes music more abundant, we believe listeners will value human artistry even more. Our job is to make Spotify the place they find it.” Jump to Comments Issa Rae’s Male Friendship HBO Comedy Pilot Casts Rafael Castillo, Branden Cook (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Girls’ Shocker: Lena Dunham Sets Revival at HBO With Allison Williams, Zosia Mamet, Jemima Kirke Returning ‘The Birds’ Reboot: Sarah Snook to Lead HBO Limited Series Take on Hitchcock Classic Bill Maher’s Embarrassing Karoline Leavitt Interview on ‘Real Time’ Trump Calls Bill Maher a ‘Complete and Total Loser,’ Tells Him ‘Don’t Call Anymore’ in Lengthy Truth Social Post ‘Lanterns’ Episode 7 Hits 7 Million U.S. Viewers in Three Days as Season Reaches Average of Nearly 19 Million Globally

title: Launch HN: Versine (YC F26) – MCP to send and receive money
abstract:
Hey HN, we’re Harshith, Param, and Vishnu and we're building Versine ( https://versine.com ). Versine lets you send and request money just by talking or texting with your AI (think Venmo with an MCP). We’re software engineers who have worked on distributed systems at Stripe, Databricks, and Amazon. Versine is an MCP that sits in front of a wallet with a balance. With it, your agent can do things like: - Send money to someone with your approval (via passkey in our app) - Send and request money to/from up to 100 people at once - Send money to people without a Versine account (they cash out to their bank in 2 mins) - Pay people without your explicit approval to trusted contacts (you can set this) Here’s a demo:  https://youtube.com/shorts/Q9X7zioEqi0  We started working on this because assistants are frustratingly hands-off when it comes to finance and money movement. You can have your assistant go through a receipt and map out all the amounts owed taking care of splitting the subtotal, taxes, tips, but at the end of it the assistant hands back work to you when you have to go out and make the Venmo transfer. Our current solution is oriented towards power users: those who want to automate everything through their agent use us to split dinners, group trips, or settle poker ledgers. We see ourselves unlocking more value for the general consumer as 1. More people turn into power users of agents, and
2. We expand to a more complete banking solution: deposits, transfers, wires, everything you can (and more) do with your bank offered as an MCP. Behind the scenes, each user has a self-custodial stablecoin wallet storing USDC on Base. With self-custodial wallets, users own their keys, meaning money can’t be sent without their approval. Interestingly, we were almost forced into this solution because we had around 4 weeks to build this product (after a pivot), and traditional fiat with a partner bank would have caused far too many regulatory and compliance slowdowns. Because of that, the only fast option that remained was using stablecoin wallets. It also ensures we aren't a Money Services Business (MSB) since we don’t hold control or access to the user’s funds. Each call to the wallet creates what we call one-time or recurring standing permissions. For a one-time payment, your agent makes an MCP call, and you receive a notification in our mobile app. Once you swipe up in the app and approve with a passkey (or your device’s biometric method), we create a one-time permission that instructs your wallet to send $X to your recipient’s address. Trusted contacts let your agent send money to people that you’ve previously authorized without explicit passkey approval. Generally, these are people that you’d trust to send your money back even if your agent made a mistake. We’re also able to support sending money to someone off Versine using claim forwarding, where the user authorizes us to forward a specific amount to a future address (which we create once we verify a recipient's OTP). Param worked on scaling vector search at Databricks and harness evals at Glean. Harshith worked on core Stripe Connect fee-processing infrastructure and built an AWS Fargate autoscaler at Amazon. Vishnu worked on intent-based agent testing infrastructure at Amazon. None of us were experienced in stablecoin or crypto infra before working on Versine but our distributed systems experience has helped us a lot. We'd love for you guys to try it! It's available on iOS and Android and as an MCP on ChatGPT and Claude. We also support a public MCP and REST API for other agents. Please let us know how you find it and if it works as you'd hoped!  https://versine.com

title: Show HN: Mason – A lightweight Postgres read-replica, built on columnar storage
abstract: Hi HN! TLDR: we’ve built an open-source drop-in replacement for a postgres read-replica, powered by duckdb’s columnar compute engine. It’s very fast. And it looks like postgres. So, this started out as: let’s just connect Clickhouse to our postgres dbs and throw our analytics queries at it instead. That will speed everything up.  But we quickly found that 1) Clickhouse comes with quite the learning curve (engine optimisation) to make it fast (we needed something we could easily drop in to any customer’s postgres scenario), and 2) we had underestimated how different clickhouse’s SQL syntax was to postgres.  Don’t get me wrong: we love Clickhouse (it’s ridiculously fast if you know what queries to expect), it just didn’t work for our ad-hoc postgres workloads. So we went searching for alternatives that were 1) more plug-and-play and 2) looked a lot more like postgres. We dismissed a bunch based on desk research alone: - pg_mooncake (seems to have stalled since data bricks bought them) - pg_duckdb (seems to offer fast queries, or fresh data, but not both - we needed both) - materialize/risingwave/readyset (like Clickhouse, they require knowing the query shapes upfront - not ideal for ad-hoc workloads) - firebolt (license makes it challenging to offer to our customers) - redshift / alloydb / etc (we wanted something cloud-provider agnostic) And we shortlisted 3: - pg_clickhouse (Postgres extension that parses SQL in Postgres and pushes the work down to ClickHouse) - cedarDB  (closed-source, Postgres-compatible analytical database) - duckdb  (open-source, embedded columnar analytics engine with a Postgres-like SQL dialect) We needed to know how they would perform on real postgres queries, so we took a backlog of 5,410 (hand-written) queries (chosen because they had been slow to execute against postgres) from 159 real postgres databases.  We then generated synthetic data (dynamically using the schemas from those 159 databases) to fill 159 local databases so we could run the experiment. We then spun up the 3 short-listed tools locally, and ran each of the 5,410 queries against both postgres and the 3 tools, and compared the results: - pg_clickhouse (matched postgres 59.4% of the time, refused 39.9% of the queries and was “wrong” 0.8% of the time). - cedarDB (matched postgres 88.1% of the time, refused 8% of the queries and was “wrong” 3.9% of the time). - duckdb (matched postgres 84.1% of the time, refused 14.3% of the queries and was “wrong” 1.6% of the time). Matched meant they returned exactly the same result as postgres.  Refused meant they returned an error message (usually telling you some syntax isn’t recognised). And “wrong” meant they didn’t return the same results as postgres.  I appreciate that arguably postgres may be the one that is wrong in some cases - but for our use case, we considered postgres the golden source of truth. So, both duckdb and cedardb performed pretty well (correctly handled more than 80% of the postgres queries we threw at it), out-of-the box.  But we really still wanted to try and cover that long-tail. We chose duckdb as its open-source license would allow us to easily work on the long tail to get the postgres SQL parity we wanted. So, Mason (linked above), is what we built, powered by duckdb, which now matches postgres on 96% of our 5,410 queries, plus hundreds of other queries that we added, testing it with Metabase, Grafana, Superset, DBeaver and Trevor.io.  For the remaining 4%, it errors with a nice clear message telling you how to rewrite your SQL. We’d love your feedback on what we’ve built.  Useful?  How can we make it better?

title: Active intrusion campaign against Check Point security management servers
abstract:
GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries. ‍ Campaign Summary GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally. We are tracking this set of threat activity as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) which represents adversary infrastructure, tools and post-exploitation action against the 22 victims. The campaign targeting does not appear to be focused on any specific geography or industry sector. The impacted orgs include victims with assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the United States. The victim orgs sit in sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing. We do not attribute GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group at this time. We do not currently have enough information to make assessments relating to the motivation of the actor or alignment to a nation-of-origin. The actor used 99 IP addresses, much of which were disposable network infrastructure to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control of its victims, including the use of a compromised server acting as an “operational relay box” (ORB) or more simply, a “hop,” for interacting with downstream victim assets. The actor used this relay box / hop to save command results and data stolen from 24 distinct Check Point Security Management Servers. The actor used Nmap , Chisel , Impacket , Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. The threat actor used or attempted to exploit multiple CVEs, including, but not limited to: CVE-2026-61500 (Rejetto HFS), CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF). Though we observed hands-on-keyboard activity, we believe that like most modern attacks, the actor used LLMs and agentic systems to perform vulnerability scanning, exploitation, tool development, and automated interaction with compromised assets. Our visibility into this attack activity stopped around November 2nd, 2026, but given the actor’s persistent access to victim Check Point devices, we expect that this intrusion campaign is ongoing. We are working with international government partners and CERTs to share relevant intelligence and notify the victims. ‍ Observed Attacker Activities We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). ‍ HFS Scanning and Exploitation The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500 . 2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password. Example POST to loginSrp1 and response Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested ‍ 2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server. Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie ‍ Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits. 2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th. ‍ Establishing the Operational Relay Box / Hop 2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations. Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server. ‍ Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine. The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration. Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay. 2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets. The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel , and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy. ‍ Intrusion Operations and Exfiltration Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims.

title: Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Max Tegmark
abstract:
News Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Top MIT Physicist Apparently they discuss overthrowing the US government after a few drinks. by Clare Hymer 24 November 2026 Novara Media Employees at US artificial intelligence company Anthropic openly talk about “overthrowing the US government” and “taking over the world”, a world-renowned physicist has claimed. In an interview with Novara Media , Max Tegmark, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said: “When I talk to people who work for Anthropic, after they’ve had a couple of drinks, the conversation often gets into overthrowing the US government and taking over the world.” “They tend to not use words like ‘coup’ and ‘overthrow the US government’. They instead use the code phrase ‘alignment without control’,” he said. ‘Alignment without control’ is the idea that AI should be kept in check by being instilled with certain values – likely those shared by Anthropic, Tegmark said – rather than being directly controlled by humans. “We get the sort of future that Alan Turing predicted, where it’s going to be Anthropic’s machine-god running Earth, and then the rest of us just have to hope that somehow it’s gonna be nice.” Turing, widely regarded as the founder of computer science, famously warned in 1951 that once machines started thinking, we should expect them to take control. Tegmark said the comments from Anthropic staff should alarm anyone who cares about democracy. “These companies really don’t seem to like it [democracy]. They have lobbied really hard to even prevent any meaningful government oversight of them,” he said. He added: “Here in the US, OpenAI and Anthropic are less regulated than a sandwich shop.” Novara Media has approached Anthropic for comment. Tegmark’s disclosure comes as protests against AI are ramping up across the world. As Anthropic started trading on the stock market at a staggering $2tn valuation on Thursday, protesters gathered at both the Nasdaq exchange in New York and the firm’s San Francisco headquarters demanding an AI development slowdown. On Saturday, over 1,000 people marched against “AI extinction” in London in what campaigners said was “the biggest AI safety march in history”. Clare Hymer is head of articles at Novara Media.

title: From words to work: how AI social language boosts productivity and creative self-efficacy
abstract:
While AI agents enhance productivity, they may also threaten human autonomy and creativity in collaborative tasks. Balancing efficiency with individual capability development is key to advancing human–AI collaboration.
 
 
 
 Based on Emotions as Social Information theory and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this research conducted two studies to explore how AI social-oriented language influences perceived collaboration outcomes, specifically perceived work productivity and creative self-efficacy. Study 1 employed a questionnaire survey in general work and life collaboration contexts. Study 2 employed a simulated interaction experiment involving specific tasks.
 
 
 
 Study 1 demonstrated the positive effects of AI social-oriented language on both perceived work productivity and creative self-efficacy, with perceived AI-supported autonomy mediating these effects. Study 2 further supported these relationships and revealed the boundary conditions of task type. Specifically, for creative tasks, highly social-oriented AI language enhanced both perceived AI-supported autonomy and collaboration outcomes, whereas for routine analytical tasks, these effects were not significant.
 
 
 
 This study not only addresses current concerns regarding collaboration performance but also highlights the human-centered value of AI by emphasizing creative potential. It bridges the gap by linking AI language style to these concrete outcomes. The findings enrich the understanding of AI language design in human–AI collaboration and provide both theoretical and practical implications for optimizing AI interaction strategies to improve collaboration outcomes.

title: S³: A Multicriteria Pre-Deployment Scoring Protocol for Enterprise Small Language Model Selection
abstract: Technology managers lack a systematic protocol for determining which enterprise workloads are safe for local small language model deployment. We introduce S³ (Suitability Score for SLM Selection), a multicriteria framework that scores workloads across six dimensions, Task Complexity, Output Structure, Stakeholder Risk, Data Sensitivity, Latency Tolerance, and Volume Load, and assigns them to Pure SLM, Hybrid, or LLM-Only tiers before inference. Non-compensatory gate rules enforce safety constraints for high-stakes scenarios, ensuring that life-critical or expert-level generative tasks are never assigned to a local model regardless of their aggregate score. Thresholds calibrated on an independent use-case set correctly predicted all eight held-out tier assignments across six industries, with Pure SLM tiers achieving at least 95% LLM parity.

title: CineAct: Interaction-State Agents for Playable, Branching Film Generation
abstract: Open video generators such as MiniMax-H3 produce short clips of only several to a dozen seconds per run. To synthesize longer sequences, existing methods either rely on agentic systems following preset scripts, or roll out autoregressively from the previous clip's last frame, losing off-screen states and accumulating hallucinations across turns. Consequently, users still cannot take an explicit goal, choose how to accomplish it, and see that choice persist across subsequent clips. We study goal-grounded interactive video generation, where one goal admits multiple valid approaches, the user's chosen approach must be executed on screen, and its consequences must persist across clips. To this end, we propose CineAct, a state-first agentic framework in which language-model agents handle reasoning while frozen image and video generators serve purely as renderers. Before interaction, the Architect initializes the world as a spatial layout with cameras, an asset library, and a scene graph; at each turn, the system deduces the planned state change, generates a target end frame with an image generator and rigorously verifies it, and synthesizes intermediate motion with an FL2V model. We further introduce a multi-space benchmark covering two suites: long-horizon step execution and open-intent branching admissibility. Experiments show that explicit world-state modeling boosts multi-step rollout consistency over the pixel-only baseline (+11.4 automated, +23.1 human points) and raises paired branching success toward a shared goal by +30.8 points.

title: FiRE: Fine-grained Ranking Evaluation for Machine Translation
abstract: Developing reliable machine translation (MT) systems hinges on our ability to distinguish superior translations from inferior ones. However, existing evaluation paradigms, whether limited to coarse overall rankings or misaligned with human preferences, fail to deliver interpretable, fine-grained feedback in reference-free settings. We present a Fine-Grained Ranking Evaluation method (FiRE) that leverages off-the-shelf large language models to perform criterion-driven pairwise comparison across three complementary dimensions: faithfulness, fluency, and consistency of style, instead of producing a single holistic judgment. To enable rigorous meta-evaluation of evaluation paradigms in the absence of any suitable testbed, we construct the first human-annotated, reference-free benchmark for fine-grained ranking evaluation, achieving substantial inter-annotator agreement. Through meta-evaluation on this benchmark and existing MQM datasets, FiRE demonstrably outperforms regression-based and error-analysis metrics in aligning with human comparative judgments, while providing more informative insights into translation quality. Finally, our examination of LLM evaluator biases (position and self-enhancement) and their handling of tied cases offers guidance for more nuanced MT evaluation. Code and benchmark resources are available at https://github.com/wygao8/FiRE-MT.

title: Embo-Harness: Towards Understanding Frontier-Model-as-Policy Harness
abstract: Frontier multimodal models exhibit extraordinary generalization in generating robot actions from observations and instructions, enabling a new paradigm in which they serve directly as policies within closed-loop robotic harnesses. However, the design principles of such harnesses, and the capabilities underlying their strong performance, remain unclear. We present Embo-Harness, a framework for systematically studying frontier-model-as-policy harnesses. We investigate four components of the robotic agentic loop, namely, prompting, planning, action execution, and tool use, and distill six empirical findings into a practical recipe. This recipe prioritizes interfaces that exploit the model's native visual reasoning and tool-use capabilities over handcrafted plans, skills, or action priors, and identifies effective choices for action representation, chunking, reasoning effort, visual observations, short multi-action sequences, and policy refinement. On RoboLab-120, Embo-Harness achieves an 83.3\% success rate, outperforming the strongest reported baseline by 26.2 percentage points. It also succeeds in 15 of 20 zero-shot trials across four real-world manipulation tasks. Beyond performance, controlled interventions indicate that the studied model depends more strongly on accurate spatial target estimation than on explicit low-level joint or trajectory generation. These results provide both a practical recipe for building strong frontier-model-as-policy harnesses and a clearer account of the capabilities that drive their performance.

title: ESGPT: A Data-Centric ESG Language Model with Unified Instruction and Benchmark Resources
abstract: ESG analysis requires complex language understanding across diverse sources, including corporate reports, news, and disclosures, for tasks such as ESG relevance detection, action interpretation, impact analysis, and question answering. However, existing ESG datasets are fragmented by task and source, with heterogeneous formats and annotation schemes, limiting their use for training general-purpose ESG LLMs and unified evaluation. In this work, we construct ESG-Instruct, a 30,000-instance ESG instruction dataset built from public ESG resources, and ESGU-Bench, an ESG understanding benchmark covering six representative ESG tasks. Based on these resources, we further develop ESGPT, an 8B ESG-specialized LLM, and evaluate it against diverse open-source and API-based LLMs. Experimental results show that general-purpose LLMs exhibit substantial performance variation across ESG tasks, while ESGPT, despite its relatively small scale, achieves the best performance on multiple ESG tasks. This work provides unified data and benchmark resources for training and evaluating ESG-specialized LLMs.

title: Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance
abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating register-transfer level (RTL) code from natural-language specifications, their reliability remains limited on designs with complex control logic and temporal behavior. This stems from a fundamental semantic gap: high-level natural language often leaves implementation-critical details underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer unstated assumptions. This paper presents Layered Formal Guidance, a novel framework that bridges this semantic gap by using formal properties as an intermediate semantic layer between natural-language specifications and RTL generation. Our framework applies formal guidance across three layers: property-driven specification augmentation before generation, property-consistency checking after generation, and counterexample-guided refinement after checking. Experiments on RTLLM benchmarks and various open-source IP designs demonstrate that our framework achieves higher functional correctness and lower sampled output-trace diversity. Furthermore, we show that Layered Formal Guidance can flexibly augment both general-purpose LLMs and domain-specific models to substantially improve their generation reliability.

title: Intent-Conditioned Argument Mediation for Tool-Using LLM Agents: Blocking Trusted-but-Unauthorized Arguments
abstract: LLM agents turn a user's request and retrieved content into tool calls, and a call can reach the wrong recipient, endpoint, file or participant. Argument-level provenance blocks such values when they come from untrusted content, but accepts a trusted value that the user never requested. IntentFlow, a mediation layer between an unmodified planner and its tools, checks each authority-bearing argument against an intent contract and a provenance policy. On a synthetic benchmark of 200 attacks (oracle intent and injection labels, declared roles), attack success falls from 50.5% with provenance alone to 12.0% [8.2-17.2%]; every remaining success alters a content or payload field. IntentFlow wrongly blocks none of 200 paired benign tasks and 4 of 50 hard ones. On 50 trusted-but-unauthorized attacks, provenance-only mediation executes all 50 and IntentFlow none; a CaMeL-style check also blocks all 50 but rejects 16 of 50 benign tasks. On an offline AgentDojo-derived replay, IntentFlow blocks all 20 attacks at 75% benign success, as does a CaMeL-style check; a Progent-style allowlist blocks 19 and keeps all benign tasks. With one live planner and the same oracles, the mediator blocked all 17 corrupted calls proposed in 110 attacks.

title: TrialAgentBench: Evaluating AI Agents for Clinical-Trial Analysis and Long-Horizon Drug-Development Decisions
abstract: Clinical drug development is a long-horizon, high-stakes process requiring sequential decisions based on information that costs money and time to acquire. AI agents have demonstrated capabilities for scientific analysis, but there is no established way to evaluate them on these decisions, as real trials are expensive, involve people, and never reveal the counterfactual. We introduce TrialAgentBench, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on clinical trial analysis and drug development decision-making using simulated trials where the truth is known, embedded within the data records of a fictional drug sponsor. We publicly release nearly 3,500 tasks, varying from analysing a single trial to managing multi-phase programmes with budget and time constraints. We score each analysis by rerunning its code on new trials, and each programme by the value its decisions achieve. Across 24 closed- and open-weight models, the strongest agents can analyse raw, messy trial records to within 6% of a process-aware analysis, even when an assumption is violated, with 95% confidence intervals containing the true effect 94--95% of the time. Over the prior year, the best model improved from 19% above this analysis, with serious misses on 15% of tasks, to 3.5% and 1%. What limits them is decision-making from evidence under uncertainty: when to correct, what evidence to buy, when to stop. The strongest agents are overly careful, correcting on 83% of tasks with equal recording errors, where it is unnecessary. On drug programmes, the best agent has substantial headroom, reaching 48% of the value an oracle achieves against 58% for a rule-based developer, with others falling 24 to 66% short. Model generations show ongoing improvements in handling data and evidence, with substantial variation. The strongest models can act as competent analysts, but do not yet make reliable long-horizon decisions.

title: Visual-RFT++: Extending Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning to Multimodal Tool Use
abstract: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) has recently become a central paradigm for advancing Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), as demonstrated by systems such as OpenAI's o3 and the R1 series. Despite significant progress in LLMs, how to leverage RFT to unify visual perception, step-by-step reasoning, and agentic tool use into one coherent training paradigm remains an open challenge. In this work, we present Visual Reinforcement Fine-Tuning++ (Visual-RFT++), a unified framework that extends RFT to both visual perception tasks and multimodal agentic workflows, enabling LVLMs to reason with images, act upon images, and evaluate their own outputs using verifiable reward. With Visual-RFT++, open-source LVLMs not only show significant gains on diverse visual perception tasks, but also acquire agentic abilities such as web searching for real-time information and code-based image manipulation (e.g., cropping, rotation, and analysis). Across visual perception tasks, including fine-grained classification, few-shot detection, reasoning grounding, and open-vocabulary detection, Visual-RFT++ delivers strong gains over SFT, including a +24.3 percentage points improvement in one-shot fine-grained classification and +21.0 percentage points on COCO's 4-shot setting and +15.4 percentage points on LVIS with around several hundred samples. To evaluate agentic behaviors, we introduce the Multimodal Agentic Tool Bench (MAT) with MAT-Search and MAT-Coding. Visual-RFT++ surpasses its baseline by +18.6 F1 / +13.0 EM percentage points on MAT-Coding and +10.3 F1 / +8.7 EM percentage points on MAT-Search. It also shows gains of 29.3 F1 and 25.9 EM percentage points on multi-hop QA benchmarks such as 2Wiki and HotpotQA, demonstrating strong cross-modal generalization. Visual-RFT++ introduces a data-efficient and reward-driven framework that strengthens both visual reasoning and agentic adaptability.

title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
abstract: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.

title: TRAE: Trustworthy Automated ESG Annotation via Multi-Agent Consensus and Confidence Assessment
abstract: With the growing demand for ESG disclosure and evaluation, constructing high-quality datasets for automatically extracting ESG-related information from large-scale documents has become essential. However, ESG annotation remains challenging due to strong context dependence, ambiguous label boundaries, and the need for domain expertise, resulting in high annotation cost and limited scalability. To address these challenges, we propose TRAE (TRustworthy Automated ESG annotation), a multi-agent framework for scalable and reliable ESG data construction. Unlike direct LLM-based annotation, TRAE evaluates annotation reliability by modeling agreement, confidence, and reasoning consistency among multiple agents through a structured multi-step reasoning process. Experimental results demonstrate that TRAE improves annotation performance compared with existing automated annotation strategies. Furthermore, TRAE supports a hybrid human-AI annotation strategy that assigns expert labeling only to uncertain samples, reducing annotation cost while preserving data quality. Using TRAE, we construct a high-quality ESG dataset containing approximately 20,000 instances with complete reasoning traces, intermediate agent outputs, and reliability information to enhance transparency and reproducibility. Overall, this work provides a practical and scalable framework for trustworthy ESG data construction. The code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/nowzer0/TRAE.

title: Beyond Binary Correctness: A Surrogate for Confidence Learning in Large Language and Vision-Language Models
abstract: Confidence estimation for large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) aims to assess how likely a particular generated response is to be correct. We investigate how learning this assessment can benefit from the model's predictive reliability on the underlying query. Binary correctness supervision, however, assigns identical labels to occasional errors and frequent failures, as well as isolated successes and consistent success. These outcomes can arise from substantially different predictive behavior under stochastic decoding. We propose a confidence-learning framework that supplements realized response correctness with query-level predictive reliability. We estimate reliability through repeated generations under a fixed model and decoding configuration, then combine the empirical success rate with individual correctness to construct a graded confidence surrogate. The surrogate differentiates responses sharing the same correctness label while preserving the average predictive reliability of the sampled response pool. To learn this target, we condition an independent confidence estimator on the query and its full generated response, and optimize backbone LoRA adapters together with a projection and scalar confidence head using mean squared error. Repeated sampling is required only for supervision construction; inference scores an individual response without additional generations. We establish ordering and mean preservation properties of the surrogate and derive a selective-risk bound connecting population surrogate prediction error to the error rate among accepted responses. We evaluate the framework across language and vision-language models, examining confidence calibration and selective prediction.

title: Parameter-Efficient Vocabulary Expansion via Cross-Lingual Embedding Alignment
abstract: Continual pretraining with vocabulary expansion is often used to make large language models (LLMs) more effective and efficient at handling new languages. However, when LLMs are extended to many languages simultaneously, the number of model parameters increases significantly. In addition, the newly added tokens do not receive the same number of training steps as the tokens in the original vocabulary, which sometimes causes vocabulary expansion to yield only limited performance improvements. We propose leveraging the semantic equivalence between words in the model's primary language and those in the extended vocabulary to transfer learned representations. In this paper, we introduce MATE, a parameter-efficient vocabulary expansion method that enables effective cross-lingual transfer with 8 times fewer additional parameters per token. MATE reduces the average tokenization compression ratio and delivers improvements on multiple benchmarks.

title: Hard to Translate, Harder to Detect: Human Analysis Remains Essential in AI Meme Translation
abstract: We present a dataset and evaluation setup for a problem in creative machine translation: translating culturally loaded passages that carry much of a text's meaning and humor that may depend on subtle or implicit discourse. We study Soviet comedy quotations that function as memes in Russian-language communication. Off-the-shelf difficulty estimators do not find these passages; current models searching the web find most but not all of them, but their own analyses of the difficulty do not help translation as well as a human-validated one. Given a brief human-validated analysis of why each passage is difficult, older models improve modestly; the strongest current translators (GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5) improve more, and in human evaluation GPT-6 Sol comes close to the approved references on most films. Newer models have thus become much better at using such an analysis while still not reliably producing it themselves. We release (1) a dataset of five films'Russian subtitles with their audience-selected culturally salient passages, human-validated analyses, and reference translations (into English, Galician, and Spanish), together with every full-film LLM translation and evaluation produced in this study; and (2) an item-level MQM-style evaluation protocol that measures translator and evaluator noise to set the number of runs the evaluation needs, and whose automatic version tracks human judgment of these passages, which reference-free neural metrics do not, whether they score the whole text or the passages alone.
